speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the owners of the Usen Fisheries fish plant in Souris announced it was closing for the winter, throwing hundreds of people out of work and devastating the economy of eastern Prince Edward Island.
Because of federal fisheries mismanagement, the plant owners decided it was more economic to process redfish in Nova Scotia. People in the area are worried about their future and they want action from the federal government.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has communities fighting communities over falling groundfish stocks. This is unfair and I call on the minister to ensure the future of the fish plant in Souris. The people of eastern Prince Edward Island want to work this winter but they cannot. The government must do everything possible to allow the plant to return to its former status as a year-round employer.

Mr. Speaker, section 30.1(5) in chapter IV of Bill C-105, which concerns changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, doubly penalizes the unemployed.
It means that a claimant disqualified from receiving benefits because he voluntarily left his employment or lost his employment by reason of misconduct would be denied the right to receive benefits at the time the event occurs.
It also means that later on the following year, for instance, if this person again becomes unemployed without being disqualified on the grounds of the manner of termination of employment he would again be penalized because his case could be examined under subsection 6(3) and not 6(2), in which case he would need 20 insurable weeks instead of the number of weeks required under the variable entrance requirement to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Last October 25 through November 1 was the annual White Ribbon Against Pornography week. I was presented with white ribbons worn by concerned citizens of Our Lady of Mercy Roman Catholic Church in my riding of Sarnia- Lambton. These ribbons were worn as an expression of concern over the effects of pornography in our society.
Recently the Supreme Court of Canada unanimously upheld the anti-obscenity provisions of the Criminal Code as they apply to publications, video tapes, movies and other pornographic materials. This law is important as it is needed to protect women and children against violent and sexual exploitation.
The federal government is now considering a law on pornography and children to protect the most vulnerable in our society from sexual exploitation and abuse.
I,	along with all members of this House, am committed to fighting the violent and sexual exploitation of women and children.

February 10, 1993

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the employees of the Sudbury taxation centre are fuming over the recently announced parking fee increase which will come into effect this April.
This marks a 33 per cent increase over the two and one-half years since parking fees were first implemented and this for a parking lot that is not accessible or usable by anyone else.
I want to remind this government that these are the same federal employees, most of whom are women, who have had their wages frozen for the next two years. Once this tired old government is through after the 33 tax increases, the GST, free trade, its assault on middle class families, the unemployed and in this case parking fee increases, the concept of disposable income will no longer exist for these hard working Canadians.
This government is an advocate, I believe, of disposable Canadians, not disposable incomes. I urge the minister responsible to reconsider his decision and for this government to give Canadians a break.

Mr. Speaker, it was just a few days ago that opposition members were screaming in this House that free trade with the United States was not working because the Americans had imposed modest duties on Canadian steel.
This was absolutely no proof that the FTA is flawed. In fact without the agreement Canadians would have no opportunity to fight arcane protectionist U.S. trade laws.
Today opposition members should be admitting that free trade works because Canada has just scored another important victory using the dispute settlement mechanism of the FTA. Canadian durum wheat exports to the United States are a success story at $65 million a year. Now a free trade arbitration panel has dismissed U.S. attempts to hurt Canadian producers. This is the ninth consecutive time that Canada has won using the terms of the free trade agreement. In addition, since the FTA was implemented, Canadian exports to the United States have soared while we have gained protection from
protectionism. The least the critics can do today is thank God for the FTA.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join with others in welcoming to Ottawa members of the prairie pools who will be meeting with the respective caucuses later this day. They are here to discuss among other things the serious income crisis which is hurting Canadian farmers.
The agricultural industry is a fundamental pillar of the Canadian economy. Agricultural exports represent 7 per cent of all Canadian exports in a trade surplus of $3 billion.
Western grain farmers, Ontario com producers, the Quebec milk industry and the maritime potato farmers are living in very difficult times.
I want to tell them that for a Liberal government, farmers and agriculture will be a priority. Food security and maintaining rural life are essential to the future of Canadians. It makes good economic sense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to inform the House and underline an important report by a dispute resolution panel under the free trade agreement on Canadian durum wheat exports to the U.S.
The report, which was jointly released by both countries on February 9, concludes that the Canadian Wheat Board's pricing practices for durum wheat exports to the U.S. are consistent with the rules set out under the free trade agreement.
This ruling demonstrates the dispute settlement process does work. Much has been said on the durum issue but what counts is the panel ruling. As a result of the free trade agreement we are able to deal fairly with the concerns raised in the U.S. Canadian durum will be able to continue to move into the market.
The government has always maintained that the Canadian Wheat Board operates within the rules set out under the free trade agreement. This panel ruling of February 9 confirms this. The Canadian Wheat Board on
February 10,1993

behalf of Canadian producers will continue to take advantage of all market opportunities wherever they may be.

A shattering event took place this morning on Parliament Hill. That noted feminist and advocate for gender equality, the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, made a mistake. Worse, this Canadian Phil Donahue, this British Columbian Alan Alda, this prototypical gender sensitive nineties liberated male made a mistake about me.
Knowing as I do the hon. member's utter devotion to furthering the cause of women in politics and knowing that in his long years in politics he has probably never been misquoted, I can only suppose that he attributed statements to me that I have never made without checking with me because he is too shy, too hesitant, too totally opposed to any hint of confrontation to even approach me.
I know he will say that he read it in print. I can understand that such a naive innocent would believe everything he reads. But I am here to put him out of his misery, quick.
My office door is always open. I can always be reached by phone. I even have a surprise for the hon. member. I would be prepared to speak to him in the lobby, not the lawn, not more than once a week, but I would be prepared to speak. I promise that he will never ever have to run the risk of being so totally wrong again.
I say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker: Dave, do you want to step outside?
Let's go.

Mr. Speaker, this issue was raised in the House last week by the member for Churchill. The Queen's Journal quotes the member for Halifax, saying that she supports the North American free trade agreement because it puts Canada in a good position. She said that NAFTA is much
better than the bad deal negotiated by the Tories and the U.S. in 1988.
However, my issue today is not that. It has to do with the Minister of National Health and Welfare's lack of commitment to increasing funding for AIDS.
We cannot afford to be short-sighted when it comes to funding for AIDS and HIV. The cost in human, social and economic terms is too high. Funding for education, prevention and research in HIV and AIDS is a wise investment. It should be a question of when we spend these sums of money, not if.
Canada can dedicate adequate funds now or we can try to cut comers and pay for the far higher social and financial costs that will come later as we deal with the unnecessary, tragic and costly illnesses we will have failed to prevent.
The minister is on record saying the government must be committed to long term action. I urge the government to follow the advice of its own experts and I urge the minister to heed his own words that the government must commit itself to long term and adequate AIDS funding now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the tragic history of Kashmir.
A UN Security Council resolution in 1948 called for a plebiscite to determine Kashmir's future. That never occurred. Since then, tens of thousands have been killed or wounded. On January 6 of this year Indian forces killed more than 40 civilians and wounded approximately 100 more. This is in addition to the thousands of civilians over the past 40 years who have been subjected to arbitrary arrest, rape and torture.
In view of the world's disregard of Kashmiris' human rights and the resulting suffering, I urge the Government of Canada to strongly recommend that the UN Security Council actively pursue a solution that is in harmony with UN initiatives and the 1972 Simla accords.
Surely the principle of self-determination of which Canada has been a great supporter should be upheld in Kashmir. The long-suffering Kashmiri people should

February 10, 1993
Oral Questions
not be continually brushed aside simply because other world events occupy the world's attention.

Mr. Speaker, an Alberta RCMP officer has admitted to having sex with a woman in his police car while on duty and in his uniform. It is alleged that he may have asked for sex in exchange for not charging her with impaired driving.
Instead of focusing on the RCMP officer's abuse of power and appalling behaviour, an internal RCMP investigation checked into the young woman's sexual history. This so-called evidence was used to dismiss criminal charges against the officer who is still on duty over a year later.
I ask the Solicitor General to investigate this matter personally. RCMP officers must never be allowed to abuse their power. The Solicitor General must establish a fair method of looking into complaints against RCMP officers so these inquiries do not boil down to investigators conducting a witch-hunt on the complainant in defence of their colleagues.
Canadian women deserve much better than this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Youth); Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently I was invited by Canada Post to visit its control centre for the Quebec City division and attend the daily postal service control session.
If the public were given the same opportunity it would realize how much the corporation has managed to do in a very short time comes in response to extraordinary changes in our economic and social environment.
Furthermore, after operating with a deficit for 30 years as high as $600 million annually they have managed to eliminate this deficit by introducing control systems. They can now offer Canadians an efficient postal service at a much more reasonable cost.
I can testify to the tangible, positive results Canada Post has achieved by streamlining its spending and focusing on customer service.

Mr. Speaker, what the Tories have done with the UI Act is a continuation of the destruction the Liberals started in 1978. The then Minister of Finance is now the leader of the Liberal Party.
We have noticed that the Liberals are silent on the reduction of benefits. Why is that? Could it be because the Liberals support the 3 per cent reduction just as they did when they reduced benefits more than 6 per cent in 1978?
At that time they used all the same excuses the Tories are using now to attempt to justify their actions. At that time the Liberals took the meat and potatoes off the table. Now the Tories are taking the bread and milk off the table.
No one should trust the Liberals to be any different from the Tories when it comes to attacking the unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister of employment my question is for the Prime Minister.
For several weeks the minister of employment has stressed that if someone is transferred or changes jobs his or her spouse is eligible for unemployment insurance if they move. However, according to the regulations released yesterday, the minister says that the community's expectation that married people will live together permanently is not an absolute principle for justifying someone who quits his or her job.
Does the Prime Minister agree with the principle that a married couple should stay together?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the hon. member and members of this House, I would say that she is drawing conclusions that are incongruous, to say the least, from a document that is only a draft which I have never seen and have not authorized and which cannot change the law. I could refer the hon. member to decisions of the Federal Court of Canada which clearly
February 10, 1993

say that under the law anyone who quits a job because there is no reasonable alternative is entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. That will not change at all.

Mr. Speaker, the minister can twist and turn as much as he likes.
The fact is at the very time he was telling this House that sexually harassed women would be protected, that spouses could stay with their spouses in case of a job transfer, at the very time he was making these promises in the House his own officials were preparing regulations that did the exact opposite.
His own internal document says that a mother who has a child undergoing long-term treatment in a hospital in another city cannot leave her job to be near her child unless she can prove that no one else can fulfil her role.
How in the name of all decency can the minister ever circulate a document which would deny the necessity of a mother to be near a critically ill child?

speechtext:

The member refers to a draft document of the department as regulations in preparation. They are not regulations. They are directives that eventually I will have to endorse and approve. That has not been done.

Oral Questions
she can show that somebody else cannot actually be there to be with her child.
I know it is an issue of concern to the Prime Minister. Will he personally review the recommendations that are being circulated? Will he state categorically that any policy of the employment ministers department that would deny a woman the right to be with her dying child will be refuted forthwith?

Mr. Speaker, I really do not know why my hon. friend in seeking to make a political point would trivialize a human situation by suggesting that an official of the Government of Canada would in any way, directly or indirectly, tolerate the kind of human condition to which she refers.
My hon. friend knows, or should know there are already 40 reasons considered to be legitimate for quitting a job. They are accepted as such by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and sustained by jurisprudence. These include: sexual harassment, dangerous working conditions, obligations to accompany a transferred spouse, obligation to take care of a child, any unilateral reduction in salary, unilateral changes in working conditions, discrimination on a prohibited ground of any type of discrimination, the refusal or loss of a right to union affiliation or participation in union activity, and so on and so forth.
It is a sensible, appropriate, humane and reasonable list of realities which makes sure that the presumption is always resolved in favour of the worker. What we have is a situation accepted by many industrialized countries in the world.
My hon. friend may have a valid point from time to time but she certainly is destroying whatever validity she has today.

speechtext:

Right now in Montreal there is a two-year delay in appealing those cases.

My question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. The changes that this government has

already made to our unemployment insurance system have moved it closer to the one our southern neighbours have. In the United States the government does not fund unemployment insurance and benefits are not paid to those who quit their jobs.

My friend is mistaken. Our social programs are better than those in the United States and we intend to keep them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Not in Spain.

Now he says: "Not in Spain".
The fact is that we have the most generous social programs in the world, I think. Some countries imitate us and some have other provisions, but the Government and Parliament of Canada are keeping the highest standards for protecting our people.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
Today it was reported that the government intends to hire 300 unemployment police, also known as the Bernard macoutes, which seems to be a new federal policy. This would mean hiring another 300 people to hunt down the victims of the government's policies, at very high cost, because 300 people more with salaries and benefits might cost as much as $12 million.
Why is the government spending money to hunt down its victims instead of helping them?
Mr. Speaker, the focus of the question of the Leader of the New Democratic Party was: "The government's plan to hire 300 inspectors, 300 police". That is false.

Mr. Speaker, I quote a senior official of the employment department today who said: "There is no particular change in claimant behaviour", referring to unemployment insurance, and "it is just that if you put more resources in you catch more. It is like putting more police cruisers out on the highway. You are going to have more speeding tickets".
Instead of taking this approach to punish the victims and instead of forcing people to work in unsafe working conditions, why is the government not taking those funds to create employment in this country and stop punishing the unemployed?

Mr. Speaker, I just said that the prefatory remark of my hon. friend in French was false. It is false in English as well.
The question in respect of quotes from any anonymous employment official is one you will have to ask the anonymous employment official.
As Prime Minister I am happy to tell my hon. friend that the statement on which she based her question is false both in English and in French.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to note then that the Prime Minister is on the record as saying it is not the intention of the department to simply hire more people to punish the victims of unemployment. I accept his answer.
However, I have something to say to the Prime Minister concerning the proposed changes to unemployment insurance in general. It is clear, as it was from the previous questions, that the government is putting the onus on the employee to prove his or her case. This is
February 10, 1993

clearly an instance of the innocent having to prove their innocence rather than the opposite. If your spouse moves, you are going to have to hire a lawyer to see if you can get UI. If your child is sick, you are going to have to hire a lawyer to see if you can get UI.
I challenge the government to answer why it is proposing all these changes to unemployment insurance if, as the Prime Minister says, all of these exemptions already exist? Why not drop the changes and be fair to Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend in her third question very generously accepts my answer and then proceeds to change the context.
In French the hon. member began by referring to 300 police who are going to inquire, les enqueteurs. There is no such thing. I have indicated in both English and French that is false. The entire question therefore I think ought reasonably to fall.
My hon. friend asks perhaps legitimately about concerns as to how the unemployed might be protected. I pointed out to the opposition spokesman that there are 40 reasons that exist and that are viewed as legitimate for quitting a job and continuing to receive unemployment benefits.
Then why change the law?

My hon. friend says why change it. It is because they range from sexual harassment all the way to a new position classification resulting in a lower pay for the employee. The protection for an employee is absolutely comprehensive.
The question that arises is a question that I suppose could be fairly debated: Is it appropriate in a society like ours that someone without provocation, without reason, without justification of any kind, quits and walks away from his or her job and asks ordinary Canadian taxpayers to pay for unemployment insurance.
It may be that we should have a social program to look after that kind of a situation, perhaps a universal social program. It is not unemployment insurance, it is not
Oral Questions
insurance against unemployment, it is a wilful act of an individual to walk away from his employment.
Therefore, I tell my hon. friend that the unemployed are totally covered pursuant to these changes, and I think generously and appropriately covered.

Mr. Speaker, talking about learning from other nations, hopefully our Prime Minister can learn from some of these. Europe has committed itself to a $30 billion infrastructure program; Japan has committed itself to at least a $40 billion infrastructure program; President Clinton, whom he met last week, will commit the United States to a $32 billion infrastructure program.
I want to ask the Prime Minister this question. Will Canada commit itself today to rebuilding its roads, sewers, bridges, towns and cities, and put thousands of people back to work?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend refers to commitments by Europe. That, of course, is misleading information. It is totally misleading. At the Edinburgh summit certain amounts were discussed. They have not been accepted or implemented in any way in regard to stimulative spending; in fact, they are encountering an enormous number of difficulties.
President Clinton has yet to announce any program in the United States. However, someone who has announced this kind of a program, the Minister of Finance of Canada, expended $2 billion on a pro-active program on December 2. On a per capita basis that would amount to some $25 billion in the United States. They are talking about a $20 billion expenditure there.
I think we have done our share, although I would be happy to hear from my hon. friend about what more we could do and how we can finance it.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps we will take the Prime Minister up on his challenge, if he would bother to read our position on the infrastructure program.
Canadian municipalities are looking for confidence from this government. Municipalities such as Halifax,

February 10, 1993
Oral Questions
Montreal, Toronto and Calgary, London are prepared to put their money where their mouths are, as are the provinces, in a one-third, one-third, one-third program.
If the federal government had the guts to have confidence in the Canadian municipalities and workers instead of penalizing the unemployed, we could put people back to work and rebuild our towns and cities.

Mr. Speaker, that was quite interesting.
My hon. friend, in response to my inquiry about how it was going to be financed, said to read their position on infrastructure. That is like reading Ripley's Believe It Or Not. I thought in reading the position on infrastructure the member said that it would be financed out of the proceeds from their GST, the new GST.
I point out to my hon. friend we have a situation today where we have the lowest inflation rate that we have had in Canada in 30 years. We have the lowest interest rates that we have had in Canada in 20 years. We are going to lead the employment growth of the OECD and we are also going to lead in economic growth.
My concern with the otherwise intelligent suggestion of my hon. friend is what took place with our NDP friends in Ontario where they announced a billion dollar NDP job plan which created 675 jobs. That is not the way you create jobs. You create jobs by lowering interest rates and by lowering inflation.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. As you all know, the government has a legal and moral obligation to pay its fair share of municipal taxes. Canadian taxpayers do not have the option of cutting back on the amount of federal, provincial and municipal taxes they pay when times are tough. Neither should the federal government have the option to do so.
Why is the government refusing to abandon its arbitrary plan to cut $80 million in revenues from municipal coffers by freezing grants in lieu of taxes?

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works will be in the House on Monday. I spoke to him late last evening in regard to this matter. He has been meeting with the mayors and leaders of Canadian municipalities. No doubt he will be happy to respond in greater detail to my hon. friend during the course of the next week.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that. I want to ask the Prime Minister if he can do this for us.
If it is true that leaders of municipalities and the minister are meeting and that there is a lot of work to be done on the calculation and the formula itself, will the Prime Minister undertake to ask his officials to work in consultation with Canadian municipalities? At the same time as a measure of good faith, will he cancel the freeze on grants in lieu of taxes until this whole situation is cleared up?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister just said, the Minister of Public Works met with municipal leaders yesterday and that was not what they asked for. They understand the situation.
We have doubled payments to municipalities in lieu of taxes in the last six years, from some $217 million to $438 million, almost half this year. They understand the fiscal situation the federal government is experiencing as well and they are prepared to co-operate. The minister had a very good meeting with them yesterday and is committed to meet with them again very shortly in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, the opposition welcomes the government's announcement of yesterday that it intends to move the Davis Inlet Innu community over to the Labrador mainland.
My concern is why it takes so long for the government to act and why it only acts in response to negative reports in the international media. There are hundreds of aboriginal communities across Canada that have substandard housing, inadequate sewer and water systems, high levels of unemployment, substance abuse, family violence as well as the highest youth suicide rate in the world.
February 10, 1993

When will the government live up to its moral and legal obligation to bring the standard and quality of life of all of Canada's aboriginal communities up to the level enjoyed by other Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. He knows that the U.S. export enhancement program has cost Canadians farmers $2.5 billion. We also know that there is a bill before the U.S. Congress calling on its government to use EEP on U.S. exports to Mexico, thus directly attacking a Canadian market.
We also know that the problem of EEP was never a priority in the NAFTA negotiations. That was confirmed at committee by a chief Canadian negotiator.
My question for the minister is this. When is the government going to stand up for Canadian farmers and confront the United States of America on its export enhancement program?

It is
interesting, Mr. Speaker, that the member did not make reference to the way we confronted the U.S. over the durum panel that was announced yesterday where essentially Canada won all five counts.

Mr. Speaker, net farm income in this country is expected to drop almost $1 billion this year. Farm bankruptcies are up alarmingly and half of those bankruptcies are in the grains sector.
Faced with this economic crisis, farmers cannot understand the government's preoccupation with a continental barley market. Most farmers do not want it. If the

February 10, 1993
Oral Questions
minister has any doubts about it he can ask members of prairie pools who are in Ottawa today.
When is the government going to get its priorities straight and what is it going to do to attack the current farm income crisis?

The hon. member for Burin-St. George's.

Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions my party has demanded that instead of spending $4.4 billion to buy military helicopters the Government of Canada should send our existing fleet out for a complete retrofit at a considerable saving to the taxpayer.
February 10, 1993

My question is for the Prime Minister. Given that the Government of Canada has just sold seven of its Chinook helicopters to the Dutch government, which has in turn contracted with Boeing to retrofit those helicopters at a cost of $12.25 million each, will the Prime Minister explain to the Canadian taxpayer why this government insists on spending $88 million per helicopter for new ones instead of recycling the existing fleet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem quite frankly is that our fleet is so aged that it could not perform the job required.
We are building new frigates. Those frigates are basically useless or very low utility without helicopters. It does not make sense to have a new ship and a 40-year old helicopter that cannot operate in bad weather.
We also need new search and rescue helicopters. The EH-101 after exhaustive evaluation is the best helicopter and the most cost efficient way to satisfy our defence requirements in terms of the frigates plus our search and rescue requirements.
A briefing was given to all political parties and everybody interested. I do not know if the hon. member was at the briefing or not, but if he had been there he would know that his question today is superfluous.

Mr. Speaker, I think there are a lot of people who believe that the minister's answer is much the same.
The minister should be aware that not only has the Dutch government recognized the value of retrofitting existing helicopters, but the U.S. government has recycled over 800 of its Labrador and Chinook helicopters with the completion date being next year for the final round.
Given the recognition by the Dutch government and by the United States government that this kind of equipment can be recycled safety and efficiently, will the minister, before Canada sells off any more of its fleet at bargain basement prices, cancel the helicopter deal and put them back in the air in the right way?

The hon. member knows that it is entirely possible to recycle his 1950 Ford, but at the end of the day he ends up with an inferior vehicle than his 1992 one, and it costs more in the end. It is simple economics: we do the most cost effective thing and that is what we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Section 30.1(5) of chapter IV concerning unemployment insurance doubly penalizes the unemployed. If someone becomes unemployed again, without disqualification on the grounds of the manner of termination of employment, he will again be penalized because his case may be examined under subsection 6(3) and not under 6(2).

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General and concerns the Stephenson inquest.
Today the minister's aide, Brian Mclnnis, is reported as saying that the minister will ask the Law Society of Upper Canada to advise him on the propriety of the billings of the Stephensons' lawyer and the value of independent lawyers at inquests and that "the door is still open".

speechtext:

I have suggested that I am fully prepared to have this matter reviewed by the Law Society of Upper Canada or the Canadian Bar Association to determine whether, for example, the cost of engaging such counsel should be municipal, provincial or federal; whether there should be independent legal advice before such an engagement is taken; and whether, the account should be taxed.

Mr. Speaker, I take it that is an undertaking by the minister with respect to the Stephensons' legal costs and not the matters generally.

Last fall he significantly changed our laws to restrict parole for high risk offenders. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 68(2), the motion is deemed adopted.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to present this bill, an act respecting the establishment and award of the Peace Medal to Canadians serving with a United Nations Peacekeeping Force.

The purpose of this bill is really quite simple. It is to create a peace medal to honour Canadians who participate in peacekeeping activities anywhere in the world.
Canadians have long held the tradition of serving with the United Nations throughout the world. They are held in high esteem across this planet. In fact, Canadians were among the peacekeeping forces who won a Nobel Peace Prize for their involvement in peacekeeping a few years ago. That is something of which we are all proud. As well, there are currently peacekeeping forces in a number of countries such as Croatia, Bosnia-Hercegovi-na and other parts of what was Yugoslavia.
In this particular case the minister would award the peace medal to any eligible person to commemorate an act performed as part of peacekeeping in the world and someone who gave his or her life to keep peace in the world or died from a cause attributable to his or her service with the United Nations.

Although there is no provision in the Standing Orders, there is a provision in Beauchesne's. Citation 495.(1) states:
A minister is not at liberty to read or quote from a despatch or
other state paper not before the House without being prepared to lay
it on the Thble.
I seek the direction of the Chair. Would the Chair want members of the opposition to continually rise on points of order after Question Period to have the respective ministers table those documents? Or would the Chair wish to take notice of the provisions in Beauchesne's and remind ministers when giving responses to questions and quoting from documents that they ought to table those documents so members will be in a position to examine them in full as to what the ministers are saying?
I ask for guidance from the Chair. If the Chair wishes, members can rise on points of order, but I thought a better way to facilitate our deliberations would be if the Chair were to take it upon itself to do this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENTS REFERRED TO IN QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the same point of order, I respect my hon. friend opposite as he well knows. He is a man of some experience in this House and a man of considerable learning.
I am wondering whether his point today was triggered by the incident yesterday when the hon. member for Kamloops read from a newspaper ad and got into some discussion with the Prime Minister about the contents of that ad. The Prime Minister invited the hon. member for Kamloops to table what he was reading from. For whatever reason it appears that was not done and the Prime Minister tabled his own copy of the newspaper ad.
Point of Order
With reference to government documents which my hon. friend suggests ministers may be reading or quoting from, I know he is some years away from office on this side, in either direction one would look. It is the practice of ministers to read quotes from notes that are prepared for the purpose of Question Period. The long established practice is that ministers are not compelled to table that kind of note in the House.
I appreciate my hon. friend knows the Standing Orders very well. He accurately pointed out that there is no reference to any such necessity in the Standing Orders. I respect his quotation from Beauchesne's. I think the Beauchesne's quotation is designed to reflect on state papers and other official documents.
In the case of multiplicity of our practice here on this side at this time, it is merely working notes that are quoted from. I do not think there is any need for such a tabling to take place.
Finally, I do not want to be argumentative or provocative. That of course is not my nature. But I did hear my hon. friend, the opposition House leader, suggest that if what he was seeking was not complied with or if it was not followed through that there was an implicit threat of a plethora of points of order. I ask my hon. friend what has changed.
It is a time-honoured practice in this place that ministers quote from prepared notes. I do not think the front bench here has departed from that practice. Therefore, first it is unseemly to hold out such an implied threat and second, there is no real need for any points of order on the matter since the practice has not changed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENTS REFERRED TO IN QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it rather humorous that the hon. parliamentary secretary and government Whip in his remarks would resort to such a tactic. I have seen it done in other institutions when one has a relatively weak case, one will deviate from the substance of the issue raised and try to take something in through the back door.
Madam Speaker, for your information, today the Prime Minister in response to a question raised by the deputy leader of our party said that there were 40 reasons with regard to denying unemployment insurance benefits. Quite rightly the Prime Minister could not read out the 40 reasons.

February 10,1993
Point of Order
The Prime Minister did have a document which no doubt was prepared with great diligence and great care by senior officials paid by the taxpayers of this country. We would think that in the interests of those concerned about the subject matter it would only be appropriate to make that kind of document available to the House. It is in no way trying to impede or lessen the enthusiasm of ministers opposite who may be trying to give indefensible answers to superbly crafted questions, nor is it in any way to suggest to the Chair that there is an implied threat of a plethora of points of order. It is merely, if the parliamentary secretary and government Whip will recall, and if he does not recall perhaps he will refer to the "blues", seeking the guidance of the Chair as to how we might best proceed.
I am not suggesting this in order to be argumentative, to use my colleague's remarks, but I am asking the guidance of the Chair as to the best way that we might proceed in order to have a fuller examination of all of the things that are being referred to in documents which are held by ministers and the Prime Minister for the purposes of Question Period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENTS REFERRED TO IN QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think I understand the new point my friend is now introducing. It is that when a minister or the Prime Minister begins to quote from a document or note or whatever that he then be compelled to table the entire document regardless of whether the material contained in it is pertinent to the question being asked. In other words, the document may contain information far beyond the scope of the question being asked.
I would ask my hon. friend whether that is truly his intent because the consequence could be to deprive the opposition of a great many lines of questioning. I would submit that if there are 40 reasons in a particular document that the Prime Minister is referring to and he gives a couple of them every day that would provide the opposition with 20 questions. I do not know whether the opposition would want to abnegate the possibility of asking 20 questions.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: the second reading of, and concurrence in, amendments made by the Senate to Bill C-54, an act to amend the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act and other acts in consequence thereof.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today and speak to Bill C-54, which amends the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act to provide enabling legislation for the establishment of promotion and research agencies for farm products.
Promotion and research activities will contribute to a more competitive and self-reliant agricultural sector by helping producers help themselves in responding to market opportunities.
Bill C-54 was passed by this House on May 1, 1992. The Senate then passed the bill on June 11 with two added amendments. This House must now give due consideration to those Senate amendments. One Senate amendment was simply a necessary technical correction. However the other amendment removed the eligibility exclusion of farm products regulated under the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
As a result of this amendment all producers in Canada, including wheat and barley producers in the Canadian Wheat Board designated area, will be able to propose the establishment of promotion research agencies for farm products.
This amendment has received support from organizations such as the Prairie Pools, the Alberta Barley Commission, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Canadian Wheat Board. The amendment does not affect the existing authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. I want to make that very clear.
Government Orders
For these reasons the government supports the amendments made by the Senate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the amendments to the check-off legislation, the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act, which come from the Senate today are ones that the government attempted to make in the standing committee when C-54 was before that committee. Unfortunately the Speaker ruled them out of order because they went beyond the scope of the bill at that time.
This legislation really provides for check-offs for agencies to be established under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act that would allow these agencies to do promotion and check-offs for research by various farm commodity groups. It is legislation that we supported.
When this legislation came to the committee it was not clear whether groups like the prairie pools and other agencies really favoured this legislation or not.
When those representatives appeared before the committee that dealt with this bill, it became clear they thought it would be desirable to make it available for farm groups dealing with wheat and barley which are under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. They would have the same opportunity to establish this kind of promotional agency.
The amendment put forward in the House was not acceptable to the Chair. It provided for an override of the legislation as it had come to the committee by an Order in Council. When the legislation went to the Senate, they were more ingenious; they simply removed that portion of the act which prohibited promotion and research agencies being set up under the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. We all know that under parliamentary procedure we can remove things from acts but we cannot add amendments which go beyond the scope of the bill.
The Senate put that forward and we have the bill back in the House. It is generally supported by many farm groups. Some do not support it. There is an ongoing concern that it is a way for the government to set up agencies to do the promotion and research government departments should be doing. In the Department of Agriculture we have seen cutbacks in the funds for research so there is some justification for that concern.

February 10, 1993
Government Orders
Groups in some parts of the country such as beef producers already have promotion agencies. The advantage of this legislation is that the check-off can be applied to imports of beef. We have a very healthy exchange in the market between Canada and the United States. If beef producers in Canada are having a checkoff applied to them to promote the sale of lean meat and so on, that check-off should apply to meat which is being imported just the same as for domestically grown commodities such as beef. That is the only fair way.
This legislation has a lot of support across the country because it puts that caveat or provision in the law wherein imports will have the same check-off applied and will benefit from the promotion that is being carried out by that commodity group.
The amendment today would apply to promotion and research into commodities produced under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, which is barley and wheat, now that the government has removed oats from the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
I might say that the base legislation is not being changed. It is legislation that provides us with supply management and marketing boards. There is a very great concern that in the whole article XI of the GATT negotiations just how strongly the government is supporting those commodities under supply management. When the Prime Minister came back from his meeting with President Clinton last Friday, there was no indication that he had even raised the question of supply management or the GATT negotiations.
A year ago this Friday, February 12, a unanimous motion was passed in the House calling upon the government to take action to secure the support of the President of the United States and the European Community to strengthen our position for legislation which is the basis or the foundation for some 35,000 producers of supply managed commodities in the dairy and poultry industries.
There is very great concern, especially with the special briefing that was provided only three weeks ago by the chief negotiators for the Canadian government. They said that their position was apparently being weakened. They had even less support for the joint resolution that was passed by the House on February 12, 1992. They called on the government to expand its support among
like-minded nations. It did not really do that because the support we had then was something like five or six countries. Now it is apparently down to only two, and we are not sure that the Prime Minister really took any effective action in his meeting with President Clinton on that issue last week in Washington.
To maintain our position and go forward on that whole issue we need his support and the support of the European Community, the main people involved in the GATT negotiations, although other countries are involved as well.
We support this amendment to section 39 by the Senate. We want to see it passed and this check-off legislation come into effect. It has been before the House now for over a year. This amendment would do what was attempted in the standing committee when the legislation passed there. I hope it will be passed and it will go forward so that the legislation can be implemented.
These agencies that will have an international aspect to them will be available to various commodity groups across the country. In a global market situation we need agencies that can promote those commodities and provide a check-off equally for commodities being imported as well as those being produced at home.
We are supporting this amendment as it has been returned to us from the Senate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not agree with the motion as presented from the Senate. I believe it has misinterpreted the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board. I believe it already had the power to spend money on research and promotion.
Promotion is its chief reason for existence. It is a marketing agency that promotes Canadian wheat and Canadian barley of various types and for various uses around the world. In my opinion it now has the power to introduce research projects which will produce and test new varieties and new plants to meet the requirements of consumers around the world.
Therefore I did not see any use for this particular amendment. The Conservatives and the Liberals in this Chamber and in the other Chamber have decided that such a change needs to be made so I will not oppose it for an undue length of time. However I wish to state my position quite clearly before we allow this bill to be passed in a moment or two.
February 10, 1993

It seems to me the basic reason behind the particular amendment was a second-thought position of the government. It originally decided to leave wheat board grains alone, understanding I presume that the wheat board would do an adequate job of research, development and promotion of various types of crops in the wheat and barley areas.
That position changed and the reasons given usually had as part of the argument the fact that the Alberta Barley Commission would like this amendment, the barley growers would like this amendment and the wheat growers were anxious to have such an amendment.
This gives the minister and those organizations the option of attempting to get a check-off on all wheat or barley as the case may be to aid in the promotion of the organizations and their particular usage for research and promotion.
I made the point previously and I will make it briefly now. That type of promotion and research is an extremely inefficient use of farmers' funds. I pointed to various similar groups in existence where the amount that actually arrives for real research is much less than 50 per cent of the funds collected. Most of those funds are used to promote the organization and its causes rather than to do any real research in making a better grain or better product or better commodity.
I still feel that the best source of funds would be for the Canadian Wheat Board to finance such projects internally. It already has the administrative ability and I believe the legal ability to do this.
The Canadian Wheat Board in the past has financed such diverse changes as hopper cars to improve the transportation system. It has financed the education of young doctoral candidates studying disciplines useful to the wheat board in its marketing and research capacities. It has gone into the promotion of different varieties of grains in the wheat and barley classifications. I believe it could have carried on quite well without this amendment.
However, as I said, the Liberals and Conservatives in both Houses by a very large majority have decided they want to give these opportunities for various commodity groups to take check-offs, even though the money will not be spent very efficiently. That decision has been made.
Government Orders
I am in a minority and recognize that I am defeated and will permit this bill to go through, even though I still oppose the idea.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to talk about this bill. My colleague from Algoma put it in the context of farm marketing boards and they are living in a great deal of uncertainty these days.
The feeling in the agriculture industry is that the government is softening its position. A discussion like this is very timely right now. It is just a week or so short of a year when we had a rally of about 40,000 farmers here. I think it was on February 21 last year.
Since that time I believe the government has been using a lot of double-talk. It is saying: "Oh yes, we want to strengthen Article XI at GATT. We want to lend strength to that". Why does it not just come out and say: "We want to support you, plain and simple. We are behind you. We will go to the wall with you on this". Instead of that it is being fuzzed over a little bit by double-talk.
There is a great deal of uncertainty out there. I have a letter-and after listening to the discussion between the government Whip and our own House leader a few minutes ago I will be glad to table it-which was sent to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and also to the new Minister of Agriculture. It is pleading with them, asking them to give some sort of new endorsement of support. That is the basis of the letter. As interesting as the letter is, it is the letterhead that is worth noting. The letter comes from the Canadian Broiler Hatching Egg Marketing Agency, the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency, the Egg Marketing Agency, the Tiirkey Marketing Agency and Dairy Farmers of Canada.
Those are five agencies in Canada that are making a little money now. It is one of the glory spots in the agricultural industry. Not every aspect of agriculture is making a little money. Why are they making a little money? It is because they have an organized, controlled marketing system. It is worth supporting and I hope when those ministers receive their copies of that letter dated February 1 they will give some measure of guaranteed support to those who are negotiating on behalf of the marketing boards.

February 10,1993
Government Orders
The government has done this in the past. I have a quote from The Globe and Mail of December 7, 1991: "Canada's farm marketing boards will survive international trade talks now taking place in Geneva". That quote was made by the current Minister of Agriculture. Of course, he was not the Minister of Agriculture then. Would he say that today? I wish he would. I think there would be certain assurances if the new Minister of Agriculture would make that statement which he is attributed to have made a couple of years ago in The Globe and Mail.
I have another one from the current minister of fisheries who at that time said: "Canada intends to continue its supply management system". I wish that the current minister of fisheries who was in a different role when he said that-it is a quote from The Globe and Mail way back-would come out today and make that kind of statement. That would seem to be reassuring for an industry that is operating in terrible uncertainties right now. In addition to the five agencies asking for an update, a current renewed approval from this government, we find that the government is hedging. It is talking from both sides of its mouth on this one.
All the farmers are asking for is the kind of assurance they thought they were given about a year ago. My colleague from Algoma referred to that also. All parties in the House said they supported farm marketing boards.
We are at a critical stage in the negotiations. What would be wrong with saying that again? There are about
36,000	dairy farmers waiting to hear it. There are about 2,300 or 2,400 poultry farmers waiting to hear it. It does not have to be a flamboyant statement, just a statement, a repetition of what was said here approximately one year ago. They are not going to settle for anything less than that. They thought they had the assurance of the government at that time and they just need reassurance.
There is a clipping from the National Farmers Union with reference to the Japanese government and its position on imported rice which says that the Japanese government has maintained a staunch defence of its highly protected rice market regime which it considers essential not only to national food security but also to the social objectives of its agricultural industry. I think we have social objectives for our agricultural industry and they are just as important to Canadians as the Japanese social objectives for its agricultural industry would be.
I do not know why the government is hedging on this. It would seem to me it would not be unusual to come out and repeat the kind of assurance that it has given farmers who are working under the marketing boards
and also working under a great deal of uncertainty in that industry these days. They are looking for reassurance from the government.
