speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-95, an act to continue the Farm Credit Corporation and to repeal certain acts in consequence thereof, be now read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Natural Resources envelope.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak on Bill C-95. We hope this bill will be passed in all stages today rather than going to the Committee of the Whole House. We will see how the time goes.
Bill C-95, the Farm Credit Corporation Act is replacing the old Farm Credit Act passed in 1959 and the Farm Syndicates Credit Act passed in 1964. This bill will update FCC's legislation and give the corporation the flexibility to adapt its financing instruments to the evolving needs of the farm community.
We all know from our debate yesterday and other debates we have had in this House before that it is very necessary. We know and recognize that the parliamentary committee is changing, not only in this country, but throughout the world.
Bill C-95 is another example of the ongoing commitment of our government to the farm sector in Canada. There is no greater symbol of the strength and resilience of this country than the Canadian farm. The preservation and development of rural Canada has always been a priority of this government. This is another part of the Growing Together paper that was started by one of our previous ministers of agriculture after the last election.
February 10, 1993

The working groups on farm finance and management recommended that the Farm Credit Act be amended to increase FCC's operating flexibility in their 1991 report. This recommendation was supported by all interested groups during the consultative process.
Bill C-95 will give the FCC the latitude to offer financing instruments to assist farmers to compete in a global marketplace. This legislation will allow the FCC to broaden its target market and widen its range of services to better serve farmers and rural Canada.
I would like to highlight some of the key elements of the proposed legislation and show how it will strenghten the agriculture base in Canada. The Farm Credit Corporation will be able to focus its attention on value added production and diversification into other entreprises located on the farm, as well as traditional farming operations.
Part-time farmers and farmers with other full-time occupations will be eligible for loans in recognition of the shift to alternative sources of income. It will also provide those who are working in the hope of becoming involved in agriculture the opportunity to supplement their income when they first start to farm. It was a problem in previous legislation when the corporation was unable to make loans in those situations.
Today those who wish to enter farming on a small scale basis with the hope of eventually becoming full-time farmers will be able to qualify. This will be of great assistance to them.
Financing will be extended to the agribusiness areas which supply and serve farm businesses. Such entreprises as farm supply businesses and abattoirs, for example, could qualify for financial assistance. In addition, agricultural support industries, such as livestock trucking businesses and grain cleaning facilities could also be eligible for this financing. I am sure there are many other areas which we have not even thought of.
For the FCC to adequately serve these new markets, the corporation's mandate needs to be expanded beyond its traditional role. The Farm Credit Corporation will continue to contribute to growth and stability in rural communities through financial services for value added financing, diversification through non-farm businesses, agribusinesses and the rural development initiatives.
The Farm Credit Corporation will play a vital role in co-ordinating other federal farm finance initiatives directed by rural development, as well as co-operating
Government Orders
with other financial institutions and organizations in supplying financial services.
To tap into these new markets and deliver these new services, the corporation will consult the farming community to offer products tailor-made to the conditions inherent to farming.
This new act will also increase Farm Credit Corporation's administrative flexibility to respond quickly to changes in the marketplace. For example, the corporation will be able to set and offer interest rate changes more quickly in response to the financial markets rather than waiting for an Order in Council each time the bank rate changes.
It will enable the Farm Credit Corporation to accept a greater range of security instruments rather than being restricted to primary security of mortgages on rural property. For the farmer this will mean a greater range of options to meet his financial requirements with the corporation.
Finally it will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to increase the limit on loans offered to meet all of the projects and objectives we have mentioned.
The government is proposing the deletion of subsection 4(5) during the clause-by-clause review of this bill. It had been included to provide greater certainty of the corporation's jurisdiction over its own property.
However, this constitutional question is now before the courts and will be decided there. Therefore ths clause is no longer necessary in that legislation.
There is perhaps no better way to illustrate the need for this legislation than to set examples of actual situations throughout the country where new financing tools can be matched with the initiatives of innovative farmers.
In Horsefly, British Columbia, a community of 426 people, cow-calf operations are the mainstay of agriculture and one rancher is teaming up with a local abbatoir to supply beef to nearby communities.
In working with both the rancher and the abbatoir operator the Farm Credit Corporation could develop a financial package to suit their specific capital needs.
Cut Knife, Saskatchewan, is a town of 600 people located west of North Battleford serving 135 area grain farms. Cut Knife entrepreneurs plan to build a flour mill and a pasta plant adding value to the production of wheat in the area. The corporation could assist in meeting the special finance needs of these vertical

February 10, 1993
Government Orders
integration product projects of local farmers and business people.
In Winnipegosis, Manitoba, the capital requirements for agriculture, including commercial fishing and fish farming, must be met to maintain existing operations and provide the basis for expansion.
Financing this activity could be achieved through a memorandum of understanding between the corporation and an agency like the Manitoba Agriculture Credit Corporation of western economic diversification. In La Patrie, Quebec, a village of 357 in the eastern townships silviculture plays a key role in maintaining the rural community.
The Farm Credit Corporation could finance equipment purchases using loans to terms approximating the useful life of equipment on the security of promissory notes, cattle mortgages or lease to own arrangements.
My farm example takes us to Drummond, New Brunswick, where the economy is based on agriculture and forestry. Farm operations are expanding to include the production of fresh broccoli for export. The FCC's ability to lend beyond the farm gate in this community would provide producers and processors with financing for packaging and marketing initiatives.
These are but a few examples of the potential revitalization that will be assisted with the passage of the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
This legislation would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to continue to provide an effective alternative source of credit for the current and future needs of Canadian farms with the flexibility to grow and keep pace with the industry it serves.
This proposed legislation will allow the Farm Credit Corporation to deliver the products needed by the farming community and thus fulfil its mandate.
It would also enhance the competitiveness and profitability of Canadian farmers while creating vital economic activity in rural Canada for the benefit of all Canadians.
We are always trying to find ways to enhance the income of farmers and we believe that this is another tool that will be beneficial to the future of agriculture for the long-term planning and viability to meet the balance
of the years in the 1990s and to prepare ourselves for the challenges that will be there in the year 2000.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words this afternoon on Bill C-95, the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
This is a major change and rewrite of the farm credit act, the former act, and we support the bill in principle because we think it does a lot of the things that perhaps should have been done four, five, or six years ago.
I listened to the parliamentary secretary and he told us a great deal about the kinds of things that could be done under this new act. What he failed to mention was that essentially over the last five or six years we have seen the Farm Credit Corporation effectively going out of business. If we look at the number of loans in 1987-1988, not going back to how many there were in 1984 or 1985 when this government came to power, we see there were 72,182. In 1991-92, which I guess is the last fiscal year report, we see that the number of farm credit loans out there is 59,845. That is a very dramatic drop from the number of 13,000 less mortgages.
Clearly if that is the direction this government is moving regardless of the fact that we have a new act that is going to be more flexible and have a number of advantageous arrangements, if the amount of dollars is going down as it has gone, the amount of mortgages it holds has gone from $4.7 billion to $3.5 billion. That is a dramatic reduction in the amount of money that is made available.
I think the idea that legislation will provide for further processing off the farm or a group of farmers work together is very commendable because it provides more flexibility and gets us into the further processing which has been dramatically reduced in the last four or five years in this country.
I think farmers and groups will want to know if the government is willing to put more money into the industry, not take it out as it has been doing for the last five years. In fact the reduction in the number of mortgages of 13,000 is just about the number of farmers who have given up during the last five or six years and left the land completely because they simply could not
February 10, 1993

Government Orders
live with the kind of pressures that were put on them by the Farm Credit Corporation and by this government.
Clearly when we look at this legislation that is before us today I would say we have one of the most desperate situations that we have ever faced in this country in terms of agriculture. We only have to look at the situation that we saw a couple of weeks ago in Saskatoon when 13,000 farmers gathered for a rally to protest the lack of support by the government in terms of stabilizations programs.
We only have to look at the rally that was held just a week or so ago in Lucknow where 1,000 farmers gathered to protest the lack of action by the government. Underlying all that in the field crop area is the concern that Ontario corn producers feel, wheat and barley producers feel and grain producers feel in Saskatchewn. We have the uncertainty of the whole supply management sector.
We hear reports from the chief negotiator at the GATT negotiations that the government is weakening its position. If a GATT agreement is reached after the French elections next month, and while it could be that the whole underpinning or the major underpinning import controls for the whole supply management sector will be blown away in the next few years, the value of quotas will tumble to a fraction of their value and perhaps the most stable and successful sector of our Canadian agriculture industry could be destroyed.
We are pleased to see the government bringing in this legislation which is a major rewrite of the farm credit legislation but it does not really solve the problems and the tremendous uncertainty which producers face across this nation this winter.
The legislation, Bill C-95, comes mainly from the recommendations of the farm financial task force. They made a lot of recommendations. As I go through the legislation and Bill C-95 itself I see a number of the recommendations of the 1988 agriculture committee when they made recommendations about support for finances for agriculture. So it comes about from many of those changes. It will clearly provide a great deal more flexibility in the lending arrangements for the Farm Credit Corporation. The act removes many things which are really provided for in the Financial Administration Act, some of which were apparently in conflict before.
The Financial Administration Act controls many things such as the approval of the Minister of Finance for borrowing and the approval by the government of bylaws that are passed by the Farm Credit Corporation. It provides for the auditor to be appointed by the Governor in Council. Of course, it is often the Auditor General. It provides for the tabling of annual reports and corporate plans. That is the legislation that was passed in June 1984. It is the Crown corporations legislation under the Financial Administration Act. That has all been stripped away in this major rewrite of the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
Some of the powers under the new act are very similar to the existing legislation, for example it covers the cost of loans and mortgages for land and buildings. It provides for loan guarantees, which is a new feature. I do not believe that was in the previous legislation. It provides for personal property and consolidation of debts. Many of these things were in the existing legislation but often were not used unless incredible pressure was applied on the government.
Many people who have gone through the farm debt review process say that the government agencies, whether the Farm Credit Corporation or the Alberta government agency, are the toughest to deal with, often more difficult than the banks and that is pretty tough.
A major change is that this legislation also provides for the diversification of enterprises, whether it is a slaughterhouse or a seed processing plant or any new further processing. It is my understanding that the majority of the funding must relate to primary production. That is clearly an important step forward.
Producers are asking: "If we are going to have this funding for further processing will there be additional money?" When we get into major processing plants, if that money is going to be taken away from primary producers then there are other sources for that further processing. The government and the minister in committee will have to make it clear that there must be more funding.
The reduction in funding has totalled $1.2 billion over the last five years. If we keep squeezing the amount of money that is available then there is really nothing to be

February 10, 1993
Government Orders
gained because although there may be funding for a further processing plant in one part of the country it just means that several dozen or a hundred primary producers will not have any money in some other part of the country. It must be clarified by the government that there will be additional money available.
The free trade deal and the government's policy for further processing has been a disaster. In the Canadian food processing industry 100 processing plants had gone out of business since the free trade deal was passed in the fall of 1988. The government's own estimate, and this figure is almost six or eight months old, was that 34,000 jobs had been lost. I am happy to see this legislation and I think there will be an opportunity to provide this.
However we must compare that with the pressure that is put on Canadian food processors by the FTA and by the government's own taxation policy. In 1987 the government had a fast write-off for new further processing industries for food products of 50 per cent declining balance. That has been reduced to 30 per cent. Even the government's own agriculture competitive council is recommending that it be returned to the 1987 level. It also recommends that there be fast write-offs and improved incentives for agri-research because we are dealing with a global industry. If the incentives are greater in western Europe, Ireland, or the United States our producers will clearly have a hard time competing.
It is therefore important that the government not only provide this funding for further processing but also provide the fiscal and monetary policy to encourage that industry to survive. It is the second largest industry in the country and clearly incentives must be provided. If we lose further processing industry for food products we obviously lose that market. That is a major problem.
Under this legislation the FCC will have the power to set its own rates. That is beneficial. The way in which the FCC is currently run is unfortunate. It continues to lose its market share of the farm loan industry. Its rates are higher than those of the banks. We must wonder what the policy really is.
Under this act the board of directors will be increased. There will be more flexibility for security, and that is beneficial because a very large percentage of our producers work off the farm in addition to running their primary production units.
The other area that is beneficial, and I believe this was also recommended by the farm financial task force, is the provision for a grievance between the provincial government lending agencies, the private sector and so on.
It is interesting that in this legislation it provides that the headquarters of the FCC would be in Regina, Saskatchewan or any other place in Canada. The Tories lost most of their support in Saskatchewan in the last election. One just wonders, and God forbid that they be re-elected, that if they lost the rest of their support the headquarters would move to some other location. Regina has worked out to be a very good location because of the tremendous agriculture potential and work in that province. It is interesting that they have left the headquarters' location rather open. Later I will discuss why they might be doing that.
It is interesting that appointments to the enlarged board will be made by the Minister of Agriculture as approved by the Governor in Council while the chairperson and the president will be appointed by the Governor in Council. The procedure for the appointment of these directors and senior officers is the same as currently stipulated in the existing legislation. However, the proposed legislation takes away the power of the Minister of Agriculture to remove directors at any time, as deemed appropriate. It also eliminates the power of the Governor in Council to remove officers of the corporation at any time judged suitable.
It is amazing that the power of the government to remove people has been taken away. If we examine the Votes and Proceedings at the end of December we can see that there were some 54 Order in Council appointments and on February 3 there were 105 Order in Council appointments. We wonder if the government has some intention to lock people in for as long as possible.
There were such outstanding non-partisan appointments made on February 3 as Brian Peckford and William H. Neville to the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Obviously the gov-
February 10, 1993

emment is taking great care in these appointments and seems to be getting ready for something or other.
It is interesting that in this legislation the power to remove people is being removed, whether it is the Governor in Council's power to remove officers or the minister's power to remove members of the board of directors.
There are a number of beneficial elements of this legislation. They represent a number of recommendations. There are a number of things that could be improved, and I hope they will. I am sure there will be other recommendations when this bill goes before the legislative committee and we have heard from an appropriate number of witnesses.
It seems to me that the idea of an advisory board should be provided for in this legislation. There does not seem to be any provision for that. I know that the Minister of Agriculture has had an ongoing battle with the advisory board of the Canadian Wheat Board and perhaps that is why the government wants to remove the advisory board of the Farm Credit Corporation. It is useful to have an advisory board.
The argument is made by the government that the board of directors is larger but the board of directors has a statutory corporate responsibility to defend whatever it is doing. An advisory board is closer to the grass roots. It does not have that corporate responsibility. It is able to be a sounding board to reflect the feeling of the producers. There should be provision for an advisory board.
It is interesting that the Farm Credit Corporation would be able to make loans to non-Canadians and to people who are not even residents of the country. With the credit crunch that so many farmers are feeling in this country at this time, and especially if we are going beyond the farm gate and providing funding for the food processing industry, it seems to me that we should at least provide that these funds are available to Canadians or at least to Canadian residents, to landed immigrants.
Even though the board of directors is substantially enlarged, almost doubled, there does not seem to be any provision that a set number of the directors be primary producers. Even though this legislation is providing for further processing plants it seems to me that the primary concern should be and must be primary producers and that the funds available should be made available to
Government Orders
primary producers. I hope that additional funds will be provided to compensate for the fact that this is going beyond the farm gate and that it will not just have the same amount it has now because that would obviously take funds away.
The government has already chopped something like 25 per cent or 30 per cent of the funds available under the Farm Credit Corporation Act in the last five years. It should be providing additional funding as it is undertaking a responsibility beyond the farm gate.
There is no provision in the act for an appeal board. It seems to me there are always human personality clashes in any sphere of human activity. The FCC representative may fall into a situation where personalities get in the way of sound business decisions and it seems to me there should be provision for an appeal board. I hope the government will consider that when we get to a legislative committee.
The other area I want to look at is whether this legislation is strictly what it seems or whether it is the first step toward privatization. The Nielsen task force report in 1985 suggested that the government should consider privatizing the FCC, possibly into an agriculture co-operative.
Whether the government has this in mind or not, nobody knows for sure. Only the government knows. It would not be surprising. The government has moved to privatize practically every other Crown corporation. After all Erik Nielsen was sort of the philosopher king of this government for many years. His move to privatize everything that moves is clearly the direction in which the government is moving.
I cannot help but wonder if a number of the provisions are designed to ultimately be there for privatization. There is the fact that the government has moved the headquarters to Regina. That is clearly set out so it would be easy if the government proposes at some stage in the future to sell off the agency. The headquarters could easily be moved to where the rest of the banking industry of this country is located.
A number of things about this bill suggest that the government is moving toward ultimately privatizing the Farm Credit Corporation. I think that would be extremely undesirable. The Crown corporation should be expanded. It should be designed to provide special arrangements for Canadian farmers and not be just

February 10, 1993
Government Orders
another agency of government with no special responsibility except the bottom line. The agriculture committee recommended that in its report several years ago and I am sure it will be the view of the committee reviewing this. The record of the banking industry in this country as far as producers are concerned is not that great. It is a tough situation. We want to see the Farm Credit Corporation setting an objective and producers given the benefit of the doubt. We do not see that necessarily.
The rates of the FCC are higher than the private sector. Its share of the market is going down. As we see from the figures that I quoted earlier its contribution to Canadian agriculture is dropping all the time.
We support this bill. We think there can be improvements made in it. The farm community will have suggestions which will be useful to us. We want to hear from witnesses in the private sector as to how this legislation can be improved. We want to see some amendments in the legislative committee but we are pleased to support it.
We are aghast at the government's general and cavalier attitude toward the dramatic reduction in farm income that we are facing in 1993. It is almost a $1 billion reduction. We have seen the government's support programs already dropping. We assume that something will happen there.
If you look at the government funding over the years, especially for those commodities in the grain and oilseed sector, it usually comes to a peak in an election year, as happened in 1987 and 1988. It came to a peak last year compared to previous years but even that was dramatically lower than 1987 and 1988 even though world prices for grain are not much better.
We hope the government will recognize the desperate situation that thousands of producers are facing this year and provide those support programs that are required to stabilize the industry to see us through this difficult time.
We hope that the predictions of the chief negotiators at the GATT negotiations will be false and that the government will stand up and support those producers in the GATT negotiations. Otherwise we will see thousands of producers who have been self-sufficient and doing a
great job in their commodity areas of poultry and dairy facing the same kind of dismal situation which so many grain and oilseed producers have faced for these long years.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us a bill to create a new expanded Farm Credit Corporation which I approve of in principle.
It was a bit more than a decade ago in this House that I recommended to the then Minister of Agriculture, Eugene Whelan, that a farmers' bank was something that would be useful, given the situation that existed then. An expanded Farm Credit Corporation would have been able to provide credit to put in crops, to finance livestock, to finance buildings and the expansion of the farm itself, as well as the equipment and the wherewithal to expand off the farm into businesses which were integrated into the farm either forward or backward. It was a dream that I proposed to the Minister of Agriculture at that time.
That was just over a decade ago. Unfortunately we may be too late, but it is better late than never in this case. It is long past the time that the Farm Credit Corporation began to act in a way that will make it of more use to farm people than has been the case in the past.
Farm Credit, as I saw it 10 or 11 years ago, was well positioned to play the role that needed to be played in the strapped financial times farmers were facing. They were already evident in the early 1980s. Most of their credit advisers had a fairly good background in agriculture-much better than most of the banks had at that time-and they would have been well positioned to have assisted farm families in making the shift into the kind of adjustments that took place in the 1980s.
Unfortunately the Liberal government at the time did not see fit to act. It is good to see, although it is in the dying days of this Parliament and of this government, that the Conservatives have now decided to put such an agency in place.
I am not certain this new agency can still be competitive. The banks, both private and public-public meaning the Federal Business Development Bank-and the various provincial organizations that provide financial and banking services have a leg up on this new organization.
February 10, 1993

The Farm Credit Corporation is on very shaky ground at the moment financially. It will retain the backing of the Government of Canada which is a good thing because in its most recent past, if it had not had that backing it would have technically been as bankrupt as many of its clients have become. Therefore it has a big challenge in front of it to carry out the mandate this bill will give it.
I see the corporation being involved in providing loans for farms to expand into the farm supply side of their business, to allow farmers, either singly or with neighbours, to set up machinery agencies, fertilizer plants, fuel supply centres. Some of this is already being done in most of the farming areas of this country through co-operatives. This provides other options for those small communities where perhaps the co-op has failed or where there is a new alignment.
Its greatest possibilities lie in the further processing of farm products. This sort of financial institution would have been given consideration by individuals in my community who have recently set up a food processing plant which turns pea flour into a product that resembles potato chips but, of course, tastes a bit more like peas. It is healthier because it has a higher protein content and is finding a fairly good demand in the market at the moment.
Peas are grown in the area and in the future I can see the grinding of peas into flour for this further processing into what we call a chip continuing in the future.
There are a great many projects being planned and designed in the rural part of Canada I come from. Feedlots that make use of the grain to produce ethanol as a sideline with the feedlot using the by-product from the ethanol production are in place now and more are being planned. Having a source of funds from the Farm Credit Corporation is a further place for such institutions to get financing. Alfalfa dehydrating plants and further processing of food also have possibilities.
As I said at the beginning of my comments, farmers and provincial governments have provided new ways for people to act co-operatively. A number of farm communities have already figured out ways to set co-operative structures in motion that have attracted the attention of the financial institutions, including the six or seven large
Government Orders
chartered banks, to the point where some of these banks are now offering such co-operative ventures credit at less than prime.
I only mention this because it seems to me that this new expanded Farm Credit Corporation is going to have its work cut out if it is going to be a competitive institution facing the experience other lenders and other credit institutions have developed in the 10 or 12 years that the federal government sat and did nothing with regard to the expansion of powers of the Farm Credit Corporation.
I do not think we should spend a lot of time reviewing this legislation.
I approve of the parliamentary secretary's statement when he opened this debate in which he pointed out that the government intended to withdraw subclause 4(5) of the bill. It was an unnecessary part of the legislation and would probably result in a lot of political wrangling.
It is quite clear from my point of view as a federal member of Parliament who understands the need for strong federal powers over financial institutions that the final power rests with the federal jurisdiction in that regard. I do not think it had to be reasserted in legislation. That is spinning wheels and creating unnecessary verbiage and unnecessary conflict. I am pleased to see that it was withdrawn.
I will cut my remarks short so that we can go on to further stages of this bill. I believe it could be dealt with in all stages before this day's session is finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings and then the hon. member for Kent who will split 20 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have the opportunity to make some comments on Bill C-95 which is redoing the Farm Credit Corporation legislation, the act covering it.
As my colleagues have said before me I will say from the outset that I support the bill in principle. There are some ways the bill could be improved. I am not excited about the fact that it may go through all stages today because there is some work that could and should be done on it in committee. My recommendation to my

February 10,1993
Government Orders
colleagues and to the House is that indeed that should happen.
It is an important piece of legislation. I do not think we need to rush it through today. I am not saying I want to drag my feet on it, but we need to have at least a meeting or two in committee on it.
As we know it is permissive legislation and there are some good changes. One of the questions I raise is that I am not so sure that we need 12 members in total on the board of directors. I will leave it at that. I just raise that question. I am not sure we need that many.
Without going over the good things the bill does point by point, it expands the way in which moneys can be used that are borrowed from the Farm Credit Corporation by including value added parts of the industry and enterprises. In the minds of some people it may be moving away a little from what we think of as traditional Farm Credit Corporation loans for barns, machinery and land, to what I will call cottage industries, as long as they are on the farm and one of the spouses wants to get involved.
We know there is an incredible amount of stress, strain and financial pressure on the farm community today. In far too many cases one spouse has to go off the farm. As I said in the House yesterday, the average Canadian farmer feeds 120 people, but one member of the average Canadian farm family has to go off the farm to make enough money to feed the family. This will make some money available for a cottage-type business or industry that might spin off from the farming operation.
It also makes it possible for an individual to use other assets to guarantee the loan, whether that be another property some place else. In the past it had to be a first mortgage on the assets the money was being borrowed to buy. If an individual with a full-time job wants to start a farm business or livelihood in a smaller way and he has a piece of property some place else or has some investments he can use them.
It also gives the FCC the power to set interest rates. I might make a comment here that I hope with the new powers and the flexibility it will have the FCC will make the banks nervous.
There have been times in the past when maybe the FCC has been a little too lenient when it has lent money. Quite frankly there was a period of time a few years ago when the FCC was seen as the lender of last resort.
Probably some of the files it started at that time, we can say with hindsight now, were not good investments.
As the previous speaker just said, some chartered banks are lending money to agrifood operations at less than prime. If some changes in the Farm Credit Corporation can bring a bit more reality to the chartered banks and other lending institutions and therefore a little more support to agrifood and the farm community, it is way overdue. That should take place.
I become very upset every week when I get calls at my office from farm businesses that are struggling. They are working hard. They are doing the best job they can do and they say, basically with no notice, that their bankers phone them up and say their operating loans are cut. They just start tightening that old vice and the first thing we know they have restricted business to the stage that it just cannot survive any longer and we have lost it. Not only have the people lost their incomes. We in the agrifood industry in Canada have lost that input and that production.
There are a couple of places where there should be some improvements. I am not at all happy with the fact that there really is not a proviso in the legislation, unless I have missed it, for an appeal board for people who are not happy with the way they have been dealt with. I think that provision should be there.
If there are to be twelve members or directors in total, one being the chairman, one being the president and ten being directors, three of those directors should definitely be primary producers. That stipulation should be included in the make-up of the board of directors. I am not saying it would not happen, but I think the industry and I would feel more comfortable if it were there.
I have discussed the next one with the minister in the last few minutes. I do not know what the answer is. It is being checked out, but I think we should follow it up. I know there is concern-it is a concern of mine and of some other people I have talked to since this legislation has been out there-that this legislation makes farm credit loans available not only to Canadian citizens or landed immigrants but to non-Canadians and nonlanded immigrants.
People could come into Canada from another country and avail themselves of the benefits of the Farm Credit Corporation. I do not know where that fits in as far as the charter is concerned and what that would do, but it definitely does concern me and others who have brought it to my attention. In a nut-shell the feeling is that Farm
February 10, 1993

Credit Corporation loans should be available only to Canadian citizens or landed immigrants.
I do not have any other comments I would like to make. This is a move in the right direction. It is a little overdue. The industry needs a lot of help. There is a lot of uncertainty, uncertainty whether it be over GATT, whether it be over the future of the Western Grain Transportation Act, whether it be over the future as to whether barley will be in or out of the Canadian Wheat Board. I could go on and on.
Farmers want some more certainty. This is a piece of legislation that can start giving that. I stress again that I feel very strongly it should go to committee for a bit of work there and then back to the House in the not too distant future. Mr. Speaker, as you said, I will share the rest of my time with my colleague from Kent.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise today during debate on Bill C-95 respecting the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
I am personally inclined to support this bill, especially since many of the changes proposed in it are the result of the farm finance task force. Farmers have had input into this bill and I believe that on the whole they are in favour of it.
The major concern I have with Bill C-95 is the fact that it will seem to act just like a bank. The Farm Credit Corporation should be there for farmers. It is a lending institution of last resort.
If Farm Credit Corporation offers interest rates at the same or even higher levels than banks, what is the point of having a separate organization for farmers? I say that as a farmer. I have seen too many farmers go bankrupt in my day for many reasons, not the least of which being that the banks and farm credit were unwilling to take a risk and lend to a farmer in trouble.
Yes, the money has to come from somewhere, and I would be the first to applaud greater efficiency in the use of tax dollars. Farm credit uses tax dollars while banks do not, but we must support our farmers. They are faced with Mother Nature, low commodity prices and
Government Orders
global competition. We ought to use every means possible to ensure that Canada remains self-sufficient in food and retains the ability to export quality grains and oilseeds to world markets.
I think that a lot of people in Canada need educating on the importance and greatness of agriculture. Too many take it for granted. They go to a restaurant, shop at a grocery store and perhaps never once think about how that food got there in the first place.
Canadians would dramatically increase their appreciation of agriculture the day our farmers shut down and we were faced with a famine or food shelves were not stocked the way they were used to seeing them. This is not Russia; this is Canada. We must maintain and improve our farmers' ability to grow crops and food while helping to ensure a fair market price.
One of the things I favour with this new Bill C-95 is the fact it will allow farm credit greater flexibility in long-term financing. This is so important to farmers because no loan officer can base their figures on one, two or even three crop years.
If that were the case, no farmer would ever get a loan as they could be faced with drought one year and floods the next. We see that in my own riding of Kent. It seems to me that the aim of Bill C-95 is to extend and strengthen the mandate of the Farm Credit Corporation. Market conditions and the farming economy in the nineties are much different from those in the fifties and sixties.
We are competing in a global market so this legislation must have a global outlook. Today there is more emphasis on added value in the agrifood sector. This is an important departure from the existing Farm Credit Act which only allows the FCC to lend money for agricultural purposes.
For example, farm syndicates would now be eligible for FCC loans. As well, the expansion of financial services as outlined in this new bill will permit loans to people who lease farm land but do not own it. This is an important addition. If our farm land is being used for agricultural activities we ought to help the farmer to the greatest extent possible, even if he is just leasing the land. He is

February 10,1993
Government Orders
making good use of the land so the farm credit option should be available to him. Bill C-95 does that.
One thing that should be clarified is that the new legislation does not require farmers to be Canadian citizens to get an FCC loan. Why not? It is Canadian tax dollars used on Canadian farms. Is this the new globalization when foreigners can buy up our land and then be eligible for loans? I would like to know the government's thinking on that one.
The Liberal Party believes that an FCC loan should be available to a Canadian citizen or a landed immigrant.
Something brand new in this bill is the notion of giving the FCC the power to make guaranteed loans to farmers or a group of farmers for business related to their farming operation to allow value added production. Bill C-95 expands the availability of financial services to this kind of production. The loan would be conditional on proof that the input is going into farm production and where the output is part of farm production.
As long as the inputs and outputs of a diversified operation can be seen clearly, the proposed legislation will allow the FCC to provide a loan to a business located off the farm but within the rural sector.
Under the law presently in place the FCC could only make a loan to a business venture on the farm, but subclause 4(1) of the bill does not come right out and say that the value added part of the farm operation must be located in rural Canada to get an FCC loan. The legislation does not set any boundaries on population size to distinguish between rural and urban centres and yet this same subclause says the bill is for the benefit of rural Canada. Why is there not a clarification on that?
The original mandate of the Farm Credit Corporation was to lend money for agricultural purposes only. Bill C-95 is a significant departure from this. The new bill proposes to include loans to farm businesses that diversify beyond the farm gate for value added production.
I feel the result of this move while logical at first glance could mean a large percentage of FCC funds being transferred away from helping our primary producers and instead to further value added production facilities.
Clause 4(2)(a)(iv) fails to explain how the FCC will deal with problems which could arise when dealing with laws under provincial jurisdiction. For example, if a farmer obtains an FCC loan to diversify into ethanol production and then later he decides to diversify again into the distribution of ethanol blended fuels, how can we justify FCC financed oil tanks on farm land zoned as agricultural?
There are still kinks to be worked out in this bill. That may come through actual implementation.
One of the major changes in the proposed legislation is found in subclause 4(2)(g) which gives the FCC board the power to set interest rates charged on loans. Under the current law it takes six to seven days for the Governor in Council to set interest rates and fees for guarantees. Now FCC loans charge a higher rate of interest than the banks in keeping with the greater risk of farm loans.
We still must address the real problem which is the government's economic policy. Even though the FCC increased its lending by 86 per cent last year, it continues to lose market share to banks and credit unions. Many banks have adapted well to the marketplace with agricultural specialists, regional head offices and bank managers trained in farming pursuits.
Something that bears closer scrutiny is that under subclause 4(2)(h) the FCC must operate on a break-even basis. No farm credit program will be allowed if it is losing money. The only way the FCC could operate a money losing program would be for the federal government to provide farm credit with equalizing payments.
Something that is a positive move is the reduction debt to equity ratio. The current debt to equity ratio is 25 to 1. Subclause 12(3)(b) imposes a limit on liabilities to 12 to 1.
Under the current legislation the FCC would be allowed to borrow up to $28 billion, whereas under the new rules the FCC would be limited to between $13.5 billion and $16.8 billion. The reason behind increasing the FCC's capital limit and imposing a lower limit on liabilities is that the government is interested in Farm Credit growing through its own profits like any other private corporation. I certainly do not have any problem with that.
February 10, 1993

We are all very aware of the problems with agriculture today. The number of family farms has dropped steadily over the years with roughly 280,000 farms remaining today, down 13,000 from 1986.
The total farm debt has reached a staggering $23 billion. The ability to repay that debt is compounded by a farmer's low income. In 1991 farm bankruptcies reached 441, double the number from 1980. It is amazing to note that the average Canadian farmer has about $525,000 invested in the farm, yet only realizes $15,707 in annual farm income, of which over half is producer support payments by the Canadian taxpayer.
The GATT discussions are very important to farmers, especially in my area of southwestern Ontario. The future of supply management is in doubt. Marketing boards account for over a quarter of total farm cash receipts and supports 38,000 farm families.
We have a grain subsidy war on our hands and I know the new Minister of Agriculture shares our concerns. He knows that the impact of the grain subsidy war on the price of Canadian grain between 1985 and 1990 resulted in the loss of $4.7 billion in farm revenues on the export of 90 million tonnes of grain. Now under the free trade agreement we have opened the border to U.S. wheat.
I believe that the FTA failed to protect traditional Canadian grain markets from U.S. subsidy programs such as the Export Enhancement Program. According to the Canadian Grains Council, between 1985 and 1990 the EEP has resulted in the loss of $2.5 billion in grain sales.
In conclusion, the level of desperation in rural Canada is increasing tenfold. As established farms face foreclosure, farm families are under tremendous stress and rural communities are in decline.
Bill C-95 goes some way to increasing the flexibility required to handle the unique needs of the farmer. It moves the system into the globally competitive nineties. If in the long run it helps farmers more effectively and efficiently than the old Farm Credit Act, then I am all for it. Despite some of its imperfections, I am pleased to support Bill C-95.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I notice our colleague from Saint-Denis has joined us. I just wanted to remind all sides of the House that he has been here a long time.
It was 29 years ago today that our colleague from Saint-Denis was first elected to the House of Commons. He is one of the senior members. In a by-election on February 10, 1964 this very shy and reserved man who is reluctant to speak very often came to the House of Commons. I have a lot of admiration for him, the rather multi-dimensioned guy that he is.

We held a meeting at the Chateau Laurier Hotel. In came this effervescent young member of Parliament and he was introduced as the newly elected member for Saint-Denis. That was my first encounter with the hon. gentleman.
The point of order was introduced with a reference to the first half of his political career which is now 29 years in the House.
The riding of Saint-Denis has grown accustomed to longevity in its elected representatives. The hon. member's predecessor, Azellus Denis, was first elected to this House of Commons in 1935. political heaven after and on the basis of that, I think the incumbent for Saint-Denis is already one year overdue to find his reward in political heaven.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my colleagues in congratulating the hon. member for Saint-Denis on his anniversary. I do not envy him his 28 years. It is not something I anticipate for myself but I do appreciate the hon. member and the contributions he makes.

I too want to add my congratulations to Marcel Prud'homme, the hon. member for Saint-Denis. Marcel, I mean it sincerely.
Bill C-95, the bill before us today, amends the Farm Credit Corporation Act. This act has assisted thousands of farmers, myself included, over the years. I was a client going back a lot of years ago when I first started and later expanded.
It is a good organization and provided a service that was badly needed because back in those times we could not get a mortgage from the banks. I am happy to say that over the term of that mortgage, I believe it was 25 or 30 years, through a lot of scrounging, a lot of improvising and a lot of worry, we were able to meet our commitments. Only once or twice over that time span did we have to ask for a delay, but when we asked we were always granted that request.
I have been upset in more recent years when I see younger farmers struggling to make ends meet. I would like also to point out that we have a lot to look at in this act. As was noted in the report of the Auditor General, this is the second consecutive year the Auditor General did not have sufficient evidence to conclude that the allowance for loan losses, and consequently certain other items in the FCC's financial statement, were fairly presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.
I want to repeat that last part, that the Auditor General found there was insufficient evidence to know if the FCC's financial statements were fairly presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.
I am afraid that this bill may very well lessen the corporation's accountability to Parliament and may well lessen the ability of the Auditor General to investigate the accounting practices of FCC.
I have been approached by many producers, not just from my own constituency, but outside my own constituency. They feel they have been dealt with unfairly by the FCC. They were led to believe that all these people like themselves are malcontents and trouble makers. I am very sorry and shocked to hear this.
Just last week I was contacted by a producer who has been unable to get a proper accounting of his mortgage account history. This is a client of a corporation that has
Government Orders
to respond to the Parliament of Canada and he cannot get an accounting. He made repeated requests for the information. Until my office called the local office he was told he could get this information only by filing a court request. Yet when we requested this information we were assured that it was sent. But FCC continues to stonewall and did not send the requested information. It sent some but not what was requested.
I am beginning to feel that on this and previous situations, my role as a member of Parliament may well be infringed upon when I am asked by a constituent or someone outside my riding for specific information and ask for it in writing.
In fact I want to go back a few years to the 1988 five-year plan required by the legislation that was supposed to be tabled in this House within 15 days of the next sitting of Parliament. I had to wait three years for that corporate plan and so did this House. It was not received until nearly three years later. I suggest that my rights as a member of Parliament were infringed upon by not being able to have that information.
This particular producer wants an exception to end the date of mortgage and reamortization application of payment, with the rate of interest and how that interest is calculated in a statement from the FCC, not just a summary of the amount owing. Surely this is not too much to ask from any institution.
I do not see anything in this bill that will ensure that producers have a right to their own information when dealing with FCC. This bill really should be increasing the accountability of FCC to Parliament and to producers, not reducing it. It is most essential that accountability be available to all of the borrowers.
One also has to wonder about the removal of the provision that a future Minister of Agriculture can remove members of the FCC board. If this is so, can the government appoint a new batch of members? I also object to the removal of the stipulation that half the members of the FCC board be agriculture producers.
In another case, an individual who deals on a regular basis with FCC cases sent me a fax the other day with some interesting figures. He did an analysis of information we sent him on request. He points out that the FCC claims to have a 75 per cent rate of success in dealing with the Farm Debt Review Board. However, that figure refers to cases resolved, but resolved does not refer to cases where the applicant is allowed to continue in the

February 10, 1993
Government Orders
business of farming, but the FCC getting some sort of settlement.
In this person's mind the figure is a 72 per cent failure rate in Ontario and a 74 per cent failure rate across Canada, as only 28 per cent and 26 per cent of Farm Debt Review Board cases involving FCC result in the producer being left with a farm operation.
I do not see anything in this bill either that would direct the FCC to deal fairly and openly with the Farm Debt Review Board. All too often I have been running into the FCC using a bait and switch tactic with producers before the Farm Debt Review Board. That is the case where the producer believes they have a deal struck to make a settlement with FCC and makes the financial arrangements to do that from another source only to be told that the deal is all off now. We have something else in mind. The FCC made one deal before the hearing and another deal at the last minute, either after or during the hearing itself.
A constituent of mine whose case I raised primarily in this Chamber, in an attempt to get the FCC to deal fairly with him, wrote me a letter in November 1992 notifying me that 1,350 days after the last Farm Debt Review Board and attempting to reach a settlement with FCC, a court ruled that FCC could not liquidate him without going to court.
I want to read a section of this letter into the record that describes dealing with FCC in flesh and blood terms. I want to point out that this particular client is severely handicapped. He writes:
As with every major fork in the path the family has been forced to travel, the timing is contrived to enhance the maximum stress damage to the cohesion of the family and the individuals carrying on the struggle.
To schedule such decisions for Christmastime is no coincidence. It is also no coincidence that in an Ontario Court of Appeal before the proceedings began, the lawyer for FCC called my father a loser while looking at my father and within my father's hearing range.
That a Crown corporation answerable to the Parliament of Canada, and directed by the Minister of Agriculture, would put a family farm through a war of-5.5 years-that a Crown corporation answerable to the Parliament of Canada and directed by the Minister of Agriculture would spend or lose between $1 to $2
million doing it-are actions that the family demands be stopped,
ended, explained, corrected, compensated, published and prevented.
This is another case reported to me. The FCC arrived at the farm gate with several police cruisers just as the children of the affected family were waiting for the school bus. This type of tactic is devastating for the children, the parents and the community. Think of those children trying to explain to the other children in that school bus or at school what a group of police cruisers were doing at their farm gate just as they are going off to school when the Farm Credit Corporation was serving a foreclosure notice.
Such tactics are not acceptable for any organization, let alone an organization that operates under legislation passed in this House and supervised by this institution.
FCC is the largest single holder of land in Canada. I notice that as of December 31, it has acquired over 1,000 properties but it has over 2,500 properties on hand worth $240 million.
When you look at this sort of accumulation of properties, one has to ask about the state of mind of the people who are being forced off the land by this institution through no fault of their own.
The number of properties acquired by FCC from 1986 to 1991 increased from 324 in 1986 to over 1,000 in 1991 alone. The dollar value of properties climbed from $14 million in 1984 to the $240 million I just mentioned. That is an increase of 1,700 per cent.
This is outrageous. I worry about what lies ahead. I am sure the provisions in this bill to allow the FCC to lend money to non-Canadians so that it may dispose of the land that it has accumulated is not coincidental. Land has been accumulated from hard working Canadian farmers who are losing it not because of their own doing but because of government policies and world market conditions over which the individual has no control.
I want to go back to that letter I received in November 1992 asking how "a Crown corporation answerable to the Parliament of Canada and directly responsible to the Minister of Agriculture that put a farm family through a five and half year war with all the stress and that a Crown corporation answerable to the Parliament of Canada and directed by the Minister of Agriculture would lose between $1 and $2 million doing it". These are actions
February 10, 1993

that this particular family demand be stopped, ended, explained, corrected, compensated for and certainly be prevented in the future.
We know that times are difficult. I spoke in this House yesterday on the direction agriculture is going in the world today and that more and more huge corporations are taking over the world's food production. We see it in Canada now with two of these firms involved. I have to worry about what is going to happen not to these farmers who are having their battles now but also in the years ahead.
I suggest that we cannot hide our heads in the sand and ignore that this problem exists. As Canadians who have watched the situation develop we have to recognize it and force it to a halt. We have to make sure that food producing and processing in Canada becomes a matter of national security. I also suggest that the cases I spoke about are going to continue to multiply until such time as the Canadian producer receives a fair share of the Canadian consumer's food dollar. That does not exist at the present time.

Cornwall is not in a rural area. It is a small community of approximately 47,000 people and as such would qualify, I am sure, as a small yet urban centre. We have an opportunity in partnership to recognize the needs of our agriculture community and the potential an ethanol
Government Orders
plant would present for both the agricultural sector and job creation in the urban centre of Cornwall.
More specifically there is one site where regrettably a closure took place late last year. This particular plant offers a very sound potential site for the location of such a project. I have some serious concerns that without a clearer definition, specifically, what is a rural sector?
I would hope if the Seaway Valley Farmers Energy Co-operative people wish to make a request to the FCC for funding that they not find themselves being disqualified on the basis of the plant itself being located just adjacent to our rural area, but being of course situated yet in the city of Cornwall in an urban setting.

Once again I would hope that we would be able to clarify in that particular section of the bill as to what the interpretation might be if in fact someone came forward and asked for assistance for a loan or for a project which will go a long way into assisting particularly our com growers and so on. Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to stand here today and debate Bill C-95, the Farm Credit Corporation Act.
Farm groups across this country and farmers themselves have over the last several years experienced drastic economic problems. There is no question that all we have to do is look at the financial record of what has been going on to see a real need to revamp or change our

February 10,1993
Government Orders
financial institutions which do serve us, the farmer in this country.
I do support the move to change some of the financing institutions. I certainly would like to see a guarantee of better interest rates, a guarantee of more money and a guarantee of better financial situations for our farm community. All one has to do is realize that the total farm debt in Canada today has reached a staggering $23 billion. The total net farm income was 53 per cent lower in 1991 than it was in 1989.
In 1991 there were 441 bankruptcies. The average farm family income in 1990 was $36,900 of which only 42 per cent, $15,700, was earned on the farm. We can see in that situation off farm income provided the farm community with a much higher income than the farmer working on the farm with an investment of $1,000, $2,000, $3,000 or $100,000 could make. It really is a sad situation that we see today with extremely low commodity prices.
We see a very difficult time suffered by the farm community and not a great deal done to help ease that situation.
Many farmers in my riding really face the fact that bankers, the Farm Credit Corporation and many others have put extreme pressure on them because they are not able to service that debt on many farms.
The average Canadian farmer has roughly $525,000 invested in his farm and he realizes only $15,000 of income from that huge investment. The economic statement of 1992 cut $63 million from the western grain transportation costing the farmer a great deal more money.
The future of supply management which accounts for 28 per cent of the total farm cash receipts and supports
38,000	farm families is currently at risk because of the negotiations at GATT. That causes a tremendous amount of concern in those supply management farm families who are so concerned about the status of their livelihood today and in the future.
We really have failed that farm community as a government. We failed the farm community at the federal level. We failed the farm community at the provincial level seeing year after year very difficult structural problems.
Then, looking at some of the free trade negotiations, they really failed to protect the Canadian grain farmer from subsidy programs that the U.S. supports its farmers with. The NAFTA right now is causing a tremendous amount of threat to many of our basic producers.
As we look at the income side of farming, we see a dramatic problem that I believe this government has to address. I am pleased at this point to say that possibly there is some address here to the side of financing in the farm. There is still going to be a problem if this bill passes of raising moneys on the farming situations that we see today to pay those loans the Farm Credit Corporation may be giving our farmers.
Farm groups seem to be satisfied with many of the proposals that have come down in this piece of legislation. Therefore I feel that we should in this House support that piece of legislation. However there are some difficulties and I think those difficulties may be more clear when we start to look at the expanding practices of loans that may come about with this legislation.
The proposed bill will certainly create an over-all boader focus in the farm community and financing will be available to, as one of my colleagues stated earlier today, some cottage industry on the farm, support processing in the farm community or other activities that will be going on as diversified businesses in farming operations.
I think a great concern must be said about the numbers of dollars that are going to be available for the farm community. Will they be as high after this bill passes as they were before? I have my concerns if these loans become too diversified and move too far away from the basic producer, the basic producer may not have the access to loans that he previously would have had under this piece of legislation.
There are some areas of this new legislation that must be clarified. Does it require farmers to be Canadian citizens? As long as the input and output diversification operations are clearly identifiable the purpose of the legislation will permit the FCC to provide loans to businesses in off-farm rural sectors. However will these off-farm rural sectors start to become operations in the middle of metropolitan Toronto? Could they possibly become operations which may be moved into the urban sector and leave the rural sector in a difficult situation? Certainly, I talk about very, very large centering areas that I may have a great deal of concern about. I would
February 10, 1993

hate to see corporations like Campbells, Heinz, and other large institutions find it more advantageous to locate in metropolitan Toronto than locating in the rural communities where they are today.
I certainly realize that they have moved out of a smaller community to move into that area, which does cause me some concern. Certainly it is not to get their base product from the rural community. It is looking more at possibly importing tomato paste to move into a metropolitan area in order to service that way.
I also have some concern about loss of operations within the rural sector, within the rural communities, moving more to the large metropolitan areas.
In looking at the legislation. I believe that setting interest rates is very important. I hope as we look at the new board and its individual powers that it will take veiy careful consideration to be competitive with the banking institutions that we have in this country and have competitive rates for the farm community.
One of the problems that I have seen in the past few years is the increasingly higher and higher rates that farmers have had to pay to service loans. That has become a very important problem in dealing with the structural debt that farmers face. It is my hope that with the new structure they will be able to handle farm debt and keep interest rates in line with most lending institutions, banks, or even give the farmers a bit of a break in that area.
My final concern is that the Farm Credit Corporation will become very independent, as I see the structure being created. The 12-member board will be appointed by the government but there is no area within the legislation to take away or alter those appointments at a later date. I know of nothing in the legislation which would allow changes to occur in those appointments after they are made, which causes me a bit of concern about how independent and almost self-serving that board may become in the future. This may create some difficulty, a board that could not be controlled otherwise.
