February 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
I want to commend him on the work he has done on this bill. I see a need for such a bill. I did not only recognize this need as a member of Parliament but as a taxpayer before I ever became a member of Parliament. We always shuddered when we thought of some of the waste that was reported in the Auditor General's report.
If passed this bill with its innocuous sounding title, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act, it would radically change the manner in which the Canadian government spends its money.
The bill is a common sense bill, as my colleague from Kent says. It only makes common sense that there should be a a bill like this in the statutes of this institution because it would ensure the strict monitoring of spending by the federal government, particularly in the areas of project cost overruns.
This bill would require long-term planning on the part of cabinet ministers. They would be required to present to Parliament a detailed report showing the objectives of any proposal, the costs, the method by which this cost had been computed and its effects on the economy, the environment, employment and social programs.
Too often money for proposals is announced before the specifics of the proposal are known. This often leads to cost overruns and inflated price tags.
The Auditor General, in tabling his second report on government operations, said we needed truth in budgeting. He said: "Too often Parliament is asked for spending approval in advance with no idea what the final tab will be. Things are done on a two-step basis, a little bit now and a little bit later. We want to get away from that".
This bill would fulfil the Auditor General's intent to have truth in budgeting.
If we examine the reports of the Auditor General over the last few years we can certainly see the need for such legislation. For example, in 1991 it reported that science, industry and technology gave out $28 million to companies involved in the defence industry productivity program rather than let it lapse at the end of the year. Then it reported later that the companies involved had never asked for the money nor did they realize why they were receiving it. This is ridiculous.
This bill we are debating here this evening would stop this kind of year-end spending. If we have money left let us return it to the Treasury rather than spending it or losing it in next year's budget. We might need it next year. This attitude is prevalent in the bureaucracy.
This bill would also address situations such as one discovered by the Auditor General involving Transport Canada. In October 1988 Transport Canada entered into a 41-year lease agreement with a developer for construction of a $20 million hotel adjacent to Halifax International Airport. This project has since been terminated and only a foundation has been constructed because the department did not verify the company's financing arrangements. Important revenues were lost and future liabilities concerning this land will remain with the department.
If the department had followed the process outlined in this bill in all likelihood the error would have been caught.
I would like to offer another example from the Auditor General's 1990 report that shows why it is important that ministers, not just departments, are covered by this bill. The Auditor General found in 1990 that the Laprade Fund had been inappropriately managed since 1987 when authority for the fund was transferred to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, now the Department of Science and Technology.
In 1986, $87.3 million was set aside for contributions to economic development projects that would create permanent jobs. Approval for the funding of these projects was left in the hands of the departmental minister and one other minister. The Auditor General found that there were cases in which the ministerial approval given, the level of support given, was more than department analysis identified as necessary for that particular project to proceed.
The Auditor General also found that in one case the project was split in two and as a result received double the amount of funding approved. It is also interesting to note that all project funding went into ridings held by government members, which can only be classified as patronage.
Another boondoggle that might never have occurred if all government spending was required to be approved by the rigourous process proposed in Bill C-301 is that of the case of sky-rocketing computers.
In his 1989 report the Auditor General found that the on-line secure information communication systems program had cost overruns of close to $100 million. The project was budgeted to cost $111 million. As a result of the fact that performance specifications were not included in the contract for the project's automated
February 10, 1993

switching system the budget increased to $208.6 million in 1989.
In his 1991 report the Auditor General noted that in spite of warnings in 1987 and its inclusion in the 1989 report this particular project was not operating and the cost was an additional $53 million.
Lastly I would like to point out that if implemented this bill would stop the awarding of polling contracts without scrutiny by Parliament. It was reported in The Ottawa Citizen on January 15, 1993 that $3.2 million in polling contracts were awarded without competitive bids. It was also reported that in some instances contracts were signed after the surveys were done and the pollsters had submitted their bills.
According to The Ottawa Citizen most of the work went to two firms, Decima Research and Anderson Strategic Research. Both firms had close ties to the government. It is to put an end to such practices that a bill such as Bill C-301 is needed.
In conclusion, I would not deny that this bill requires some amendment, perhaps in committee, and that some of the details will need to be ironed out. However the principle and intent of this bill is sound. Therefore I am proud to be supporting this bill and encourage all members on all sides of the House of Commons to do likewise because, as the member for Kent says, this bill is indeed a common sense bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and to Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-301, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act.
First of all I must say that as far as I can see the purpose of this bill is to embarrass the government by shortening the time frame for the tabling of public accounts. For instance, the bill proposes that these should be tabled in October instead of December and that the Auditor General have the authority to comment on long-term planning. I listened very carefully to the hon. member who spoke before and who referred to this bill as a common-sense bill and a measure for expenditure control.
Private Members' Business
I am sure that in the House spending control has been dear to the hearts of all parliamentarians for the past 40 years. However, as hon. members are aware, it is not always easy.
It is high time the House considered this bill, which was given first reading on October 24, 1991. Hon. members have had plenty of time to analyse its implications.
Before considering the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Kent, perhaps I might briefly recall the history of this act, which dates back to 1951. It is still a very important piece of legislation and regulates a large part of the internal operations of government that form the basis for its financial administration and public-sector accounting.
To ensure the legislation remained appropriate to the needs of a government constantly adjusting to today's modern and complex world, the act has been amended on several occasions. On the last of these occasions, in May 1991, an in-depth review of the act resulted in amendments to some 70 sections.
The amendments were a response to recommendations by the Auditor General, to which the hon. member referred earlier. The Auditor General had made several recommendations. Recommendations were also made by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and the Standing Senate Committee on National Finance. The purpose of all this was to simplify the administration of public finances and bring it into line with private sector practice, to reduce the paper burden by taking advantage of computer applications-now everything is computerized to clarify certain terms both in English and in French and, last but not least, to save taxpayers money. I am sure parliamentarians on both sides of the House will agree with these goals.
However, the amendments being proposed today do not fit that mould. They are basically concerned with three aspects: the special warrants issued by order of the Governor in Council and subject to his signature, long-term planning, and the date for tabling public accounts.
As I said earlier, it is not always easy to table public accounts. As hon. members are aware, there are times when public accounts are always being held up by one of the departments. They are also aimed at providing Parliament with more specific information on the way public money is spent and bringing the time frame for

February 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
tabling the accounts more into line with practice in large publicly-owned companies.
Although at first glance these amendments seem to be desirable, I do not think it would be appropriate to adopt them. It would not be reasonable to set conditions that would inhibit the ability of the government to govern effectively and to provide accurate and quality information to this House. Let me explain.
Let us consider the first condition, which concerns subsection 30(3) of the Act. It deals with special warrants, issued by order of the Governor in Council and signed by him, to authorize payment of funds from the Treasury. The amendment to this subsection would provide that for every warrant, in addition to a detailed statement of the purposes to which the payment was applied, there should be a statement indicating the amount and the reason for the urgency.
I would remind the House that these warrants can be issued to provide the government with funds only when three conditions have been met. First of all, Parliament must not be in session. Second, there are payments to be made which are urgently required for the public good. Third, there is no appropriation to which the payment may be charged.
Some members of this House are concerned about the irresponsible use of these warrants. Actually, they are seldom used, since the occasions on which all three conditions are met are few and far between. The last time the government resorted to the use of special warrants was in 1989 in a rather unusual situation. Members will recall that following the 1988 election Parliament sat for only three weeks. Before it adjourned, however, the House had been informed of the need for further supply in the 1988-89 fiscal year. The government tabled supplementary estimates on December 16,
1988.
Later, when Parliament was not sitting, the government asked the Governor in Council to issue four warrants, on January 19, February 16, March 23 and April 1. Parliament was recalled on April 3.
Issuing these four warrants when Parliament was not in session was not at all different from the nine other cases when such warrants were issued since the Financial Administration Act was passed in 1951, 42 years ago. Considering that all in all successive governments have
issued such special warrants only 13 times, we cannot really say that the system has been abused. I believe that I can also say in all good faith that in the case with which we are concerned, the government acted responsibly in using public funds and respected the spirit and the letter of the Financial Administration Act.
The other point I would like to dwell on concerns the date when the public accounts should be submitted to Parliament. Bill C-301 would make the time limit for presenting them October instead of December.
I would remind you briefly that the public accounts show the spending on each item, government revenues and other payments credited or charged to the Treasury. They are reported to this House by the President of the Treasury Board no later than December 31 following the fiscal year-end, or if the House is not sitting, within 15 sitting days of that date.
Under the proposed amendment, subsection 64(1) of the act would be changed so that the date would be October 30 instead of December 31.
The government fully realizes that the deadline of December 31 for submitting the public accounts to Parliament is late. By then nine months have passed since the fiscal year-end. The question we might ask is whether it really takes nine months to report Canada's financial situation.
The government is the first to admit that this delay is too long. That is why it has always given high priority to having the public accounts tabled well before that deadline. Indeed, in six of the last ten years, the public accounts were tabled in the first week of November. However, we think it would be pointless to set the highly desirable deadline of October 30 in the act, and here is why.
The information in the public accounts requires a great deal of thorough, time-consuming research. This research is delayed and hindered by all kinds of difficulties. Also, the information in the public accounts comes from the departmental accounts which are not closed until two or three months after the fiscal year-end.
The departments and Treasury Board are not responsible for other difficulties that are due to circumstances beyond our control. For example, it sometimes happens that certain points are discussed with the Auditor General's office and are not settled until he tables his report. In the past this report has been tabled in October, but it
February 10, 1993

has also not been tabled until the end of November, as it was this year.
The process for drawing up the public accounts is both long and painstaking. It is detailed work and moving up the deadline for tabling the public accounts by nearly two months would only compromise the process.
I note that I do not have much time left. In a way the purpose of this bill is much more to embarrass the government than to come up with good figures. That is why I would ask the House not to go ahead and pass this bill because its purpose is much more to embarrass the government than to have accurate financial statements.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party and lend our support to Bill C-301, brought forward by our colleague from Kent. It is indeed a rare occasion that a private member's bill gets this far. One that has been labelled a common sense bill, it is only appropriate that it gets this far, and let us hope that it gets a little bit farther. I will start by dealing with what I consider to be some negatives for 30 seconds and then get on with 9 minutes plus of positives.
As the previous member indicated, I suspect this is going to take some more time for the government. It is going to create more work for the Auditor General. It is going to be a continual internal audit on behalf of the government. It may have to create more bureaucracy to deal with the mechanics of the bill, but the bottom line is that it will bring forward fiscal responsibility and accountability. We know the public demands those now.
Indeed it is an appropriate bill. If I may just read one of the clauses so that if anybody is listening he or she can relate to the common sense of the bill, clause 42.2 reads:
Where the Minister is informed that the cost of a program on which he has laid a statement before Parliament pursuant to section 42.1 will exceed the estimated cost shown in the statement for any year, the Minister shall lay before Parliament a statement showing:
(a)	the amount of the excess cost for the year,
(b)	the reasons for the excess,
(c)	the alternates that have been considered before concluding that
the excess is unavoidable.
Private Members' Business
One might ask for a concrete example or several examples and say: "Does this happen? Just how bad are the overruns when the government loses control of spending?"
I want to cite a statement I made in May 1991 talking about cost accountability at external affairs. It was noted that the estimates for external affairs revealed that between 1987-88 and 1990-91 construction sites in Algiers, Buenos Aires and Tokyo all experienced severe cost overruns.
For Algiers the increase was 169 per cent; for Buenos Aires, a mere 200 per cent; for Tokyo, 478 per cent; the Canadian pavilion in Seville, 50 per cent; the Canadian embassy in Washington, the cost overruns for those buildings out of one department of this government was $102 million. To go from the ridiculous to the sublime, the Canadian government said that it had to put a gate up at its embassy in Washington and that the gate was going to cost $170,000. This is a very special gate. We found out that it was too heavy and that it would not swing so we had to replace the gate. Perhaps that shows some of the fiscal irresponsibility of the government.
It does happen. It happens on a regular basis. What is the problem with making the government fiscally responsible and accountable to Canadian taxpayers? I am sure if they were told about these overruns on a regular basis as they happen they would be horrified. It does continue. We can go to whatever lengths are necessary to bring fiscal responsibility to whatever government happens to be in power at the particular time.
The Museum of Civilization is a classic, something of which Canadians can rightly be proud. In 1982 the estimated cost was to be $80 million. In 1985 it had risen to $122 million. In 1987 it went up another $46 million to $168 million. When we are in so deep we cannot really say: "Well, let us not proceed with this museum"; we have to finish the job. In 1988 it was just another $8 million because the designer of the building said: "Look, this building is more expensive than we thought it would be and I need my royalties to go up a little higher; my charge is going to be a little higher". It was another $8 million. In 1989 the cost of that museum started at $80 million. It finished at $340 million and it is not yet complete.

February 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
I was called over there a year and a half ago and they said: "We think the building is leaking". After $340 million, the building could have a leak in it. In fact some said there was a faulty structure and there was danger that the building was going to shake and collapse. Heaven forbid. That is veering off the point, but it went from $80 million to $340 million, a cost overrun of $260 million, and the museum is not yet complete. Once we get in that deep we cannot get out. That is the reality of the situation.
Right at the very end they wanted to get the museum opened so they said: "We had better hurry up and get all these things finished". They had to toss in another $11 million to get it ready for opening day. Unfortunately on opening day some ammonia fumes got into the museum and they had to postpone the opening. I do not know what it cost to get rid of the ammonia and straighten things out. I am sorry to have picked on such a prized structure but nevertheless that is reality. It really points to the fact that a bill like this one would bring direct accountability and fiscal responsibility to the government.
I urge the government side to support the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party in approving this bill and getting it to committee. Some say it is not perfect. Let us deal with it. Having had a bill destroyed in committee yesterday, I really appreciate that the member would like it at least to get into committee. I think it is a bill worthy of support. It should be retained, studied and supported.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate of the motion of the hon. member for Kent. I know he has put a lot of thought into it. I know his heart is in the right place. I would like to make some comments though and draw some attention to some aspects of the particular bill that need particular consideration.
Bill C-301 seeks to amend the Financial Administration Act in three areas: special Governor General's warrants, long-term planning and the tabling of public accounts. Some members may feel this is a worth-while bill to support. However many others will recognize that these changes may not be in the best interest of this House.
Allow me to respond to the concerns of the hon. member with regard to section 30 of the Financial
Administration Act which authorizes the use of special Governor General's warrants during periods in which Parliament is not in session.
Members of this House will recall how in May 1989 the House debated the government's use of special Governor General's warrants in the context of the 1989 Main Estimates. At that time the government's actions were not only determined to be in full compliance with the Financial Administration Act, but they were also determined to be fully justified.
The provision to use special Governor General's warrants under prorogation and dissolution has been provided for in our legislation since 1867. In 1951 the first Financial Administration Act was passed. That act broadened the provision to use the warrants during periods when Parliament was under extended adjournment.
The changes made have not fundamentally changed the original criteria governing the use of special Governor General's warrants. They have only clarified the scope of their application. The provisions of the Financial Administration Act which govern the use of special Governor General's warrants sets out three conditions under which the warrants may be used.
They are: Parliament must not be in session because it is dissolved, prorogued or adjourned; payments are to be made which are urgently required for the public good; and there is no other appropriation to which the payment may be charged.
I would like to review for the hon. member the circumstances surrounding the use of Governor General's special warrants in 1989. As most members of this House recall, that session of the 33rd Parliament lasted for almost two years before the general election of November 21, 1988.
Parliament was convened a mere three weeks later to complete the business of the previous Parliament. Even though the Speech from the Throne made it clear the purpose of the opening session was to deal with free trade, the government clearly informed the House of the need for further supply in the 1988-89 fiscal year by tabling Supplementary Estimates (B) on December 16, 1988.
Later when the House adjourned and subsequently prorogued, the government requested the Governor General to approve special warrants in accordance with section 30 of the Financial Administration Act.
February 10, 1993

The issuing of the four Governor General's special warrants in 1989 cannot be construed in any way to be a breach of rules or convention. Each of the three conditions as required by the Financial Administration Act for the issuing of warrants were satisfied.
The government's use of those special warrants in 1989 was consistent with the nine other instances that special warrants were used since the Financial Administration Act was passed in 1951. The government in no way extended the scope of the special warrants since the items covered by the 1989 warrants were similar to the items financed through Governor General's special warrants in 1979 and again in 1980.
I would like to make some comments regarding the proposed changes to section 30(3) of the Financial Administration Act. These changes would require the President of the Treasury Board to present a detailed statement for each warrant issued within 15 days after the commencement of the next ensuing session of Parliament.
As members of the House are aware, the President of the Treasury Board can attest to this urgency in the report to the Governor in Council. Information regarding the urgency of warrants is not required in the president's report to Parliament.
The question still remains as to whether there is a proven need for Parliament to have this additional measure to monitor expenditures. I suggest that the ministers who are accountable to this House for their decisions are the best judges of whether or not the appropriation is of an urgent nature.
Allow me to state now some observations regarding the proposed changes to section 30(5). As stated in the Financial Administration Act, the issuing of warrants must only occur when urgently required for the public good. It is the government's belief that by changing the definition of adjournment within section 30(5) from 15 days to 90 days we are not acting in the best interests of the public.
It would be a grave mistake to paralyse the government by restricting the ability to issue Governor General's special warrants when Parliament is not in session. In fact, it has been recognized that access to these warrants is necessary from time to time and under carefully delineated circumstances for the good and orderly functioning of the government.
Private Members' Business
History has demonstrated to us that these warrants have been issued in order to carry out urgent repairs to public buildings or to pay employees their due wages. I am confident that members of the House will realize the need for conducting timely repairs, should they be required, to public properties where the public is served while the House is not in session and to pay employees for doing so.
The next point I wish to address is the proposed addition of sections 42(1) through 42(4) to the Financial Administration Act. This amendment proposes that when new programs are established the government must table information regarding the long-term cost profile of that program as well as give the Auditor General the opportunity to review and to comment on this information.
This proposal has numerous flaws. Perhaps the most critical of these is that the proposed amendment would appear to be in conflict with section 7(d) of the Financial Administration Act. Parliament under section 7(d) has delegated the authority for long-term resource planning to the Treasury Board. This proposal would thus create ambiguity and work toward undermining the role and accountability of Treasury Board as the authority for solid financial planning practices within the government.
A concern also arises from the proposed requirement to table information relating to the establishment of new programs. Such public disclosure may have the effect of jeopardizing the intended result of new programs by impairing the effectiveness of the program delivering mechanism and reducing the benefit to the public. Surely this is not in the best interests of Canadian taxpayers who contribute their hard-earned money toward such programs.
This proposal also calls into question the role of the Auditor General. The proposed amendments significantly alter that role from one of being an important accountability agent within the system of government to one of being an active participant in government decision making. Decisions of this nature are to be made by the ministers.
Similar to auditors in the private sector who provide an opinion to the board of directors and shareholders, the Auditor General's responsibility is to provide an opinion to the Government of Canada and the taxpayers. The responsibility for delivering this opinion is assumed at the end of a specified period of time, not at the point before the period commences. The Auditor General's resources are already well used as it is. Any new

February 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
responsibilities would only increase the costs of the audit office which are already touching $60 billion per year. This proposal would undermine ministerial responsibility for resource management by introducing another level of governmental decision making.
The government is charged with the responsibility of delivering programs which are deemed to be in the best interests of Canadians. During the development of these programs the government consults with many groups including business and academia to design the best possible programs. The cost of these programs during these times of restraint is a fundamental consideration.
Keeping this in mind, the Comptroller General is already consulted with regard to the sound financial management of governmental programs. There is no need to spend additional taxpayer money to set up a system to second-guess a decision which has been made by those who have the responsibility to make those decisions. I see I am nearly out of time.
Thank goodness.

I regret that these comments were necessary. I regret this to hon. members opposite but I think these observations are necessary and I hope they are taken to heart. As hon. members have assumed by my comments I cannot at this time support the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise in the House today to support this private member's bill, Bill C-301, an act to amend the Financial Administration Act as proposed by my colleague for Kent who through this bill has brought some long-awaited fresh air and common sense to this House.
Perhaps, like me, it comes from the member's municipal background where one needed to but could not run deficits and get heavily in debt. In fact you had to balance your budget and be fully accountable for expenditures each and every day to the taxpayers. I believe his roots do come across in this particular bill.
A colleague from Sault Ste. Marie started to talk about the over-expenditures in the Museum of Civilization. After the next election we will probably be putting a lot of Tories in that museum so that future Canadians can view the period between 1985 and 1993 as one of the
most dismal in Canadian history, but we will let the electorate look after that.
I want to talk about a different perspective on this bill because it embodies the real essence in the purpose of what private members' bills are all about. It speaks for the people of Canada and to a government that no longer listens.
Listening to government members I have found it rather curious that it would be the Conservatives who are voting against the bill for fiscal responsibility and the Liberals and the NDP who are proposing the bill for fiscal responsibility. One would think the government would be in favour of such a bill.
Bill C-301 is a call for the federal government to be accountable to the people of Canada for the tax dollars that it spends. The federal government's yearly tabling of the budget and the accompanying estimates is no longer sufficient to accountability. The tabling of the budget and the estimates only provides for a minimal amount of debate by members of Parliament.
I believe that the Prime Minister and his cabinet are the key decision makers and that members of Parliament are really sitting on the sidelines giving brief comments on the most important decisions that the federal government makes each year.
The Auditor General in his recent report concluded: "There is a general widespread breakdown of management controls including fundamental parliamentary controls. Canadians are worried about the impact of the annual deficit and the accumulated national debt on their standard of living".
That statement rings true in many respects. This bill does not only address the issue of the government's accountability to the people, it also addresses the issue of responsibility. Who is responsible for the fiscal decisions of government? As members sitting in this House, we are accountable to our constituents for these decisions. However, how can we take responsibility when much of the information which is provided to us is not given to us by the decision makers, those in cabinet?
This bill will ensure that members of Parliament can act responsibly for their constituents. Canada is faced with a population that no longer trusts its politicians. We know that. We make promises every time there is an election. We arrive in Ottawa wanting to change things
February 10, 1993

for the better. We are accountable to our constituents who elect us.
How can we fulfil this accountability when the government we represent is not even accountable to us in this Parliament? This bill addresses this concern because it requires the government to cost out fully all the programs and expenditures before they can be implemented. Any cost overruns would require special authorization.
An important implication for this bill is that it will force the government's cabinet ministers to plan for the long term, not the short term for political expediency but for the long term. That is so people will know what the plans are, how much it is going to cost and what in fact the benefits will be to the population.
As parliamentarians we do not want a government introducing sweetheart deals or sweet deals just before an election. I believe the public is sick and tired of that kind of government. We want and they want a government that is fully accountable for the implications on the federal expenditures, the taxpayers' dollars.
This bill forces cabinet ministers to present to Parliament and the people of Canada a detailed account of the cost and the effect on the economy, the environment and the employment of any new program.
All detailed financial statements would also be referred to the Auditor General and the House of Commons public accounts committee for closer inspection.
Let me give an example. We have heard that in the public accounts committee this very day there is a tremendous amount of debate on the GST as to what those numbers really are. The members from this side of the House on that public accounts committee will tell you they are absolutely frustrated in not being able to get the right numbers as to how much GST was collected, how much GST was rebated or credited back and how many tax dollars this government is really taking in by this very bad tax that we intend to eliminate in the next election.
There are some valid points on this particular bill that bring back the whole concept of accountability and
Private Members' Business
responsibility which I believe are the hallmarks of democracy and parliamentary representation.
We are spending tax dollars on behalf of the Canadian public and therefore we must account for our spending practices. As members of Parliament and caretakers of the public purse, we must have the power to do this job effectively. The only way we can do it is for members of Parliament to have meaningful input and meaningful debate on government expenditures, on long-term planning and government tax policies. I believe that this private member's bill will do this.
I compliment my colleague from Kent who I believe has put forward a common sense bill, as he has pointed out. More important, I believe it is a bill that every member of this House should support because it talks about parliamentary reform and making members of Parliament truly what they are, representatives of the people they represent.
Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate some instruction from the Chair as to the time limitations.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member will have 10 minutes. This is a private member's bill. It is 10 minutes debate and there are no questions or comments.

I certainly am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in this debate on Bill C-301 dealing with amendments to the Financial Administration Act. My interest is specifically with regard to the final section of the proposed bill.
At the outset I should relate to the Speaker that I am particularly interested in this bill because it is of specific interest to those in my community who are involved in the small business community.
I think it is terribly important that we have an opportunity to participate in the development of the organization of Canada's economic development in a small business way. Let me say that I think it is important that this bill be given at least a fair hearing in this Chamber. Clause 4 states:

February 10, 1993
Private Members' Business
Section 64(1) of the said act is amended by striking out the words
"December 31" and substituting therefor the words "October 30".
The change to the Financial Administration Act that is being proposed here is to move forward the deadline for tabling the public accounts from the present date of December 31 to October 30.
I think that there are all kinds of opportunity for all of us to appreciate. We can as small business people and as the small business community particularly can make suggestions to the government as to how it might improve or make things more appropriate from the perspective of dealing with our particular businesses and more substantially from the point of view of how we should deal with our day to day regime.
However, it is also important to recognize that the government has responsibility to the fiscal community as a whole. That is why I would suggest that we have to take into account the entire aspect of this particular bill.
Mr. Speaker, the government, as you are well aware, is always open to new ideas about ways in which management processes can be improved and government can be made more accountable to the Canadian public. These new ideas come from a wide variety of sources. I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that views are commissioned by the government and come from recommendations of parliamentary committees, one of which I am a member, the transport committee, audits by the Auditor General and in some instances even from members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, which we have often said that we were open to. Hopefully we will have an opportunity of hearing more constructive suggestions as we move along.
Today we are debating a suggestion for changing the timing of the tabling of the public accounts which was made by means of a private member's bill put forward by a member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the hon. member for Kent. While we welcome the suggestions of the hon. member and we applaud his diligence in the pursuit of improved management processes in our country we do not always necessarily agree. That is what our democratic society is about and certainly is what this House is about. We do not always agree with ideas that are put forth. This is an excellent opportunity to suggest alternatives.
The hon. member's suggestion to bring forward the tabling debate of the public accounts from December 31 to October 30 is an example of what we on this side of the House, and myself as being a private member, not a member of the government but a member of a party who supports the government, are not in concurrence with. We do not agree with the idea and would like to put forth our reasons why.
In order to understand why we disagree with the hon. member on this point it is important to understand the context in which he is proposing to make changes to the Financial Administration Act.
I should explain that the Financial Administration Act provides the legislative basis for financial management and control in government. I hope that the House will bear with me because I am not a technical person, a technocrat, or someone who is intimately involved with the department. I do not have intimate knowledge but I can only share how I feel about this particular bill. Therefore I will ask the House to bear with me as I go through the process.
The act originated in 1991 and in that year there was passage of Bill C-91, which was entitled an act to amend the Financial Administration Act and other acts in consequence thereof.
That is obviously material that would be well beyond most of our capacities to be able to digest. It is certainly beyond my capacity to digest as an ordinary civilian who is only interested in being the representative of the people in my constituency of Fundy-Royal. The entire concept is something that we should all be concerned about. I know that we should talk about things that are somewhat more considerate of the people who we represent.
Let us go back to things that are entitling us to develop conversations with reference to the bill itself. The delays, which I am told are not important, that we have been encountering in the past years have been primarily caused by external factors mainly beyond government control.
The Auditor General has been involved with things that are of interest to all of us. We should be cognizant of his report. I would suggest that a deadline of October 30 could impede the full resolution of issues that we want to deal with in the House. For this reason I am totally
February 10, 1993

opposed to the tabling deadline of October 30. I would have to vote against any suggestions before the House saying that we should change that deadline to October 30.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to support my colleague. I certainly wish I could understand what was said by the member prior to me. Perhaps we can look at Hansard in the morning and an editor will have made it cohesive and understandable. I say that in jest. He is our colleague and I think he said at the end of his speech that he truly supports the legislation that my colleague from Kent is putting before this House.
I compliment my colleague from Kent who has brought this legislation forward. He has put this private member's bill through the whole tedious procedure that private member's legislation has to go through. His success on being able to get it on the floor of this House and to have it at this stage is truly a credit to his ability as a parliamentarian and a hard worker. I am truly honoured to be able to call him my colleague.
As I stand in the House I do not see anyone to my left. There are supposed to be 40-some members but there are not many members representing one party here tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must bring this to the attention of the hon. member. I know he has been around here for a long time so he should not make these types of statements in the House. I am sure hon. members are watching the hon. member on television and they will probably be down here very shortly and getting up on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think I mentioned any particular group or anyone in particular who was missing. I apologize if I offended the rules of the House.
I want to also compliment my colleague from Kent for the hard work that he has been doing and the leadership he has been providing. He comes from an area of Ontario that is very important in the agricultural industry which is so important to our country. It is sometimes lost in our discussions that Ontario produces the majority of the agricultural product in our country. It is an industry that needs assistance. We know that people in the agricultural industry are frugal in their operations
Private Members' Business
and they would expect that feeling to be carried on in government.
The essence of what we are discussing today can be expressed as accountability and responsibility of government actions when it comes to the spending of the taxpayers' money. It can be summed up best in the speech my colleague from Kent made in the House when he introduced the bill. I would just like to paraphrase some of his words.
He said that the notion of big government not managing our money properly is coming from farmers, factory workers, students, housewives, small business owners and teachers. The list goes on and on. "I hear throughout this country as I travel that members of Parliament on both sides of the House are not paying enough attention to the way that this government overspends. This bill will go a long way toward restoring accountability to federal programs. It is what the people of Canada are telling me. It is what the people of Canada want implemented in so far as spending is concerned".
One of the fundamental reasons for problems that existed as we were beginning to become a nation was that we were upset with the foreign power coming in and providing what I call taxation without representation. That is fundamentally what we have here today. The government takes a program and allows cost overruns in the exorbitant amounts that we have been hearing about today, without having to refer the matter back to the House of Commons for further approval. In essence it is bordering on the statement that elected members of Parliament have no say in how the government is spending its funds. That is just not what was intended in the parliamentary system. My colleague has proposed legislation that is trying to correct the dilemma we find ourselves in.
When we talk about accountability and reliability, I would like to just spend the balance of my time on one issue, the goods and services tax that was introduced.
